🤖

# Research

MI350X reaches 3.86% MFU with bf16 Triton `ragged_dot`; its fp16 XLA runs reach 2.59–2.83%. The reported ~10 ms Triton expert matmul is a bottleneck hypothesis; the current MI350X results do not include a pinned-revision profile that attributes the full step. MI300X batch 32 reached 10.3% MFU over steps 2–9 but hung at step 10, which coincides with the trainer's watch interval; the cause and sustained throughput remain unconfirmed.

**Relevant code**
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108) — benchmark flags; no watch control
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166) — trainer uses default watch configuration
- [`train.py#L641-L649`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/train.py#L641-L649) — interval selects watch computation
- [`ragged_dot.py#L341-L367`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L341-L367) — XLA/Triton selection

# Proposed Fix

1. Extend the existing benchmark PR #9693 with a benchmark-only watch interval flag (0 disables watch) and the Slurm wrapper used in the issue. Pin one post-rebase benchmark commit and the ROCm/JAX versions for every comparison. Keep the production watch default unchanged.
2. On 8× MI300X, rerun the full EP8 batch-32 configuration for 20 steps with watch intervals 10 and 0, `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla`, memory fraction 0.90, no profiler, and command buffers off. Record the step-10 outcome, median time over non-watch steps 2–9 and 11–19, tokens/s, MFU, and peak memory. Treat 10.3% as preliminary until a 20-step run completes; if both variants hang, capture the failing step's trace before changing the model.
3. At the same pinned commit, rerun MI350X bf16/Triton batch 8 and fp16/XLA batches 8, 16, and 32 with the same 20-step setup. Profile a separate run of the fastest completed configuration and report time in expert GEMMs, collectives, other kernels, and host gaps. Compare against the MI300X reference only after these reruns.
4. Use that profile to choose one next change: test `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` if communication dominates, or tune the Triton expert GEMM if it dominates. Test command-buffer types separately on a smaller shape with finite-loss checks before a full-model run; the [current ROCm setup](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/559) has produced non-finite gradients and crashes with command buffers enabled. Post each run's commit, exact command, job ID, step time, MFU, peak memory, and negative results here.

Completion criterion: a full 20-step MI350X run with finite loss and a measured improvement over the rerun bf16/Triton batch-8 baseline (previously 3.86%). #9777 already covers ROCm architecture parsing; RCCL ragged all-to-all remains unsupported in its reported test, so it is not a parallel implementation target for this issue.

comments.body:
🤖 ### MI350X bf16 matmul ceiling: 1,229 TFLOP/s in JAX by kernel time (53% of datasheet peak, 97% of PyTorch's sustained 1,261)

Commits: 265ea0f (MAMF jobs 453328, 453329), d733a95 (453334), 52cf1ee (JAX 453412), 08516a7 (JAX 453420, 453421), 6b47d18 (JAX 454529), 370d41d (JAX 454561), 704ceff (JAX 454577-454580) · GPU: one MI350X or MI300X, whole node reserved · Scripts: [`experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling) (PR #9840)

This measures how fast one GPU runs a plain dense matmul, to give the MFU numbers above a measured ceiling. Two tools ran on the same node for each GPU type: k007-002 for MI350X, k002-003 for MI300X. Both venvs install AMD's `rocm-sdk-libraries==10.0.0` wheel, which provides hipBLASLt and rocBLAS; the nodes' system ROCm (`/opt/rocm-7.2.0`) is not used for compute.

- Stas Bekman's [MAMF-finder](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py) (PyTorch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, `PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_ENABLED=1`, which benchmarks every rocBLAS and hipBLASLt solution per shape and keeps the fastest) searches about 2,100 shapes. It reports MAMF (maximum achievable matmul FLOPS): the median of the 5 fastest of 200 iterations, run in bursts of 20 after 250 ms idle. It also reports MSMF (maximum sustainable matmul FLOPS): the best rate held for 2 s under continuous load. It times each `torch.mm` with GPU events recorded just before and after the call, so its rates count kernel time only.
- `jax_matmul.py` (JAX 0.11.0) times `jax.jit(jnp.matmul)` with XLA autotuning on: 1 s of warmup, then the median of ten 0.2 s windows of back-to-back calls. It runs under `rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` and reports two rates per shape. Kernel time divides the FLOPs by the GPU time of the kernels inside each window, which matches MAMF-finder's timing. Wall clock divides them by host time, which also counts host dispatch and the idle GPU time between calls. Both are sustained rates, so MSMF is the PyTorch number to compare with.

Hardware and theoretical peaks:

| | MI350X | MI300X |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture, compute units | gfx950, 256 CUs | gfx942, 304 CUs |
| Memory per GPU (as torch reports it) | 288 GB HBM3E (294,896 MB) | 192 GB HBM3 (196,592 MB) |
| Dense bf16 and fp16 peak | 2,307 TFLOP/s, as in this issue (brochure: 2,309.6) | 1,307 TFLOP/s (datasheet: 1,307.4) |
| Node, Slurm partition | k007-002, `mi3508x` | k002-003, `mi3008x` |

The peaks are AMD's dense figures without structured sparsity. `lib/fray/src/fray/device_flops.py` stores the brochure values; the percentages below use 2,307 and 1,307 to match the tables above.

Software, identical on both GPUs:

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| ROCm user-space libraries | `rocm==10.0.0` wheels (`rocm-sdk-core`, `rocm-sdk-libraries`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx942`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx950`) from `https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/` |
| hipBLASLt, rocBLAS | 100401-8d1ae90e, 5.6.0.8d1ae90e (from TunableOp's results file) |
| PyTorch | 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, with `amd-torch-device-gfx942` and `-gfx950` 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0. `torch.version.hip` is 7.15.26333 and `torch.version.cuda` is None: a ROCm build, no CUDA |
| JAX | jax and jaxlib 0.11.0, `jax_rocm10_plugin` and `jax_rocm10_pjrt` 0.11.0+rocm10.0.0 |

| MAMF-finder | commit [0359db8](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py), benchmark version 4, auto search, default tuning |

```bash
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/jax_matmul.sbatch --dtype bfloat16 \
  --m-range 4096 20480 4096 --n-range 4096 20480 4096 --k-range 4096 20480 4096 \
  --shapes-file experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt"
```

Results in TFLOP/s per GPU, with the share of the dense peak. Shapes are MxNxK. The JAX column is kernel time, with the traced wall-clock rate of the same shape in parentheses.

| GPU | dtype | MAMF (PyTorch) | MSMF (PyTorch) | JAX best | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI350X | bf16 | 1,445 (62.6%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 (54.7%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,229 (53.3%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,178) | 453328, 454577 |
| MI350X | fp16 | 1,377 (59.7%) @ 4096x4096x20480 | 1,177 (51.0%) @ 8192x4096x14336 | 1,086 (47.1%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,047) | 453329, 454578 |
| MI300X | bf16 | 698 (53.4%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | 645 (49.3%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | not run | 453334 |

The JAX column covers a 125-shape grid (M, N and K each 4096, 8192, ..., 20480), the June model's projection shapes, and, for bf16, the 28 shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted (job 454579). By kernel time, JAX reaches 97% of MSMF in bf16 and 92% in fp16. Without the tracer, the best bf16 wall-clock rate was 1,192 at 4096x4096x16384 and 1,180 at 4096x4096x12288 (job 453420).

Measured against these ceilings instead of the datasheet, the MI350X baseline above (3.88% MFU, 90 TFLOP/s per GPU) runs at 7.3% of the JAX bf16 kernel-time ceiling. The confirmed MI300X batch-16 row (8.66%, 113 TFLOP/s) runs at 17.5% of PyTorch's MSMF; JAX was not measured on MI300X.

The MI300X run reproduces the MI300X bf16 row in [Stas Bekman's table](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/README.md#maximum-achievable-and-sustainable-matmul-flops-comparison-table) (MAMF 676, MSMF 659, PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm10.0.0): MAMF is 3.3% higher and MSMF 2.1% lower. His table has no MI350X row. His MI355X row reads 62.6% of peak, the same share as our MI350X MAMF.

The next table times the same matmul shapes in both frameworks, in bf16 on MI350X, using the shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted. MSMF is PyTorch's sustained rate after TunableOp has kept the fastest rocBLAS or hipBLASLt solution for that shape; the TunableOp column names the library it picked. JAX kernel time comes from job 454579, where XLA's autotuner picked a hipBLASLt kernel for every shape. JAX wall clock comes from job 453412, which ran without the tracer.

| Shape | MSMF | TunableOp | JAX kernel | JAX / MSMF, kernel | JAX wall | JAX / MSMF, wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 | rocBLAS | 1,052 | 83% | 1,008 | 80% |
| 4096x4096x8192 | 1,246 | hipBLASLt | 1,209 | 97% | 1,150 | 92% |
| 3584x4608x8192 | 1,237 | rocBLAS | 1,199 | 97% | 1,137 | 92% |
| 4096x4096x20480 | 1,224 | hipBLASLt | 1,179 | 96% | 1,153 | 94% |
| 4096x2048x20480 | 1,089 | hipBLASLt | 1,111 | 102% | 1,065 | 98% |
| 2048x4096x4096 | 1,080 | rocBLAS | 959 | 89% | 828 | 77% |

An earlier version of this comment read the 2-23% wall-clock gap as XLA choosing slower kernels. Most of that gap was the timing method. Wall clock counts host dispatch and the GPU's idle time between calls: on MI350X a trivial jitted op takes about 43 µs to dispatch, and the GPU idles about 12-15 µs between executions even when the host keeps ahead (job 454529). Kernel time removes that overhead. On 2048x4096x4096 it moves JAX from 77% to 89% of MSMF, and on 4096x4096x8192 from 92% to 97%. JAX's kernels are within 4% of MSMF on four shapes. Two gaps remain: 17 points on 4608x4096x7168 and 11 points on 2048x4096x4096. TunableOp picked a rocBLAS solution for both. Every GEMM kernel XLA picked in these runs carries hipBLASLt's `UserArgs` naming, and we have not checked whether XLA's autotuner considers rocBLAS solutions or whether they account for those gaps. TunableOp also picked rocBLAS for 3584x4608x8192, where JAX's hipBLASLt kernel reaches 97%.

On MI350X in bf16, the June model's projection GEMMs at 4096 tokens per GPU run at 369 TFLOP/s (k and v weight gradients, 2560x640x4096) to 1,058 (lm head weight gradient) by kernel time through JAX (job 454577). 4096x2560x2560 is the shape of the q, attention output and shared expert gate, up and down projections, and of their input gradients. It runs at 972 by kernel time and 826 by untraced wall clock (job 454529). The lm head forward runs at 1,030 by kernel time and 1,029 by untraced wall clock. The k and v projections, 4096x640x2560, run at 427 by kernel time with XLA's Triton GEMM and at 556 with hipBLASLt (next table). By untraced wall clock they run at 257 with Triton. Full list in [`snowball_shapes.txt`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt). The routed-expert `ragged_dot` and the small router, attention gate and GatedNorm GEMMs are not covered.

In bf16, XLA generates its own Triton GEMM for four of the k and v shapes: every shape with a dimension of 640, and 2560x1280x4096. Every other shape uses a hipBLASLt kernel. With `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` (job 454580), XLA uses hipBLASLt for these shapes too, and its kernels run 17-33% faster in bf16. Kernel time in TFLOP/s:

| Shape | Use | Triton (454577) | hipBLASLt, Triton off (454580) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4096x640x2560 | k and v projections | 427 | 556 | +30% |
| 2560x640x4096 | k and v weight gradients | 369 | 490 | +33% |
| 2560x1280x4096 | k and v weight gradients, fused | 514 | 664 | +29% |
| 4096x2560x640 | k and v input gradients | 471 | 552 | +17% |

Of the other 38 shapes in the Triton-off run, 33 used the same hipBLASLt kernel as with Triton on, and their kernel time moved by at most 1.6%. For the other 5, the autotuner picked a different hipBLASLt kernel in the new run (see the variation note). Under the tracer, wall clock moved the other way on the four Triton shapes: on 4096x640x2560 a call took 48 µs with Triton and 61 µs with hipBLASLt, against kernel times of 31 and 24 µs, so host-side work sets the wall-clock rate at this size. We have not measured these shapes with Triton off without the tracer. In fp16 (job 454578), XLA also picks Triton for 4096x2560x1280; we did not run fp16 with Triton off.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- fp16 is slower than bf16 for dense matmuls on MI350X: MAMF is 5% lower, JAX 12% lower by kernel time.
- The best 10 JAX grid shapes in bf16 fall between 1,179 and 1,229 TFLOP/s by kernel time (job 454577).
- Run-to-run variation on k007-002. With the same kernel, repeated runs agree closely: across the 24 MAMF shapes where jobs 454579 and 454580 ran the same kernel, the median difference is 0.3% and the largest 0.6%. Some shapes move more. 4096x4096x16384 measured 1,188, 1,221 and 1,189 by kernel time (jobs 454529, 454561, 454577), and 1,192 and 1,153 by untraced wall clock (jobs 453420, 454529). Treat differences of about 3% as noise. XLA's autotuner can also pick a different hipBLASLt kernel for the same shape in a new run. It did so for 4 of the 28 MAMF shapes between jobs 454579 and 454580 and moved three of them by 7-12% (for example 20480x4096x12288: 1,039 with a 192x320 tile in job 454579, 1,164 with a 256x256 tile in job 454580).
- Under `rocprofv3`, wall clock reads lower for shapes that take less than about 100 µs per call, because the tracer adds host work to every dispatch: 4096x1280x2560 reads 401 traced (job 454561) and 472-550 in two untraced passes (job 454529). Wall-clock numbers above say which kind they are.
- The node matters. JAX on MAMF-finder's 28 shapes ran a median of 3% faster on k007-002 than on k007-004 by wall clock, and faster on 26 of the 28 shapes (jobs 453412 and 453338). The two slower shapes, 20480x4096x12288 (-8%) and 16384x8192x8192 (-4%), may reflect XLA's autotuner picking a different kernel rather than the node: 1,043 on k007-002 matches the 192x320-tile kernel in the variation note, and these two runs did not record kernel names. k007-001 and k007-003 have not been compared. The bf16 grid's best wall-clock rate was 1,156 on k007-004 (job 453314) against 1,192 on k007-002.
- With `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`, JAX ran bf16 matmuls at 15-17 TFLOP/s, 1% of the autotuned rate (job 453316, stopped by its 45-minute limit after 99 shapes). Any hipBLASLt kernel is far faster than that, so level 0 appears to switch to a different GEMM path on ROCm, and it cannot measure hipBLASLt's untuned default choice.
- MAMF-finder's telemetry on MI350X read the wrong GPU. It samples `amdsmi` GPU 0, but HIP device 0 on k007-002 is PCI 0000:77:00, which is `amd-smi` GPU 3; `amd-smi` GPU 0 is an idle GPU at about 308 W. The MI350X MAMF and MSMF runs (jobs 453328 and 453329) predate the fix in stas00/ml-engineering#143, so their power and clock readings, the 38 MHz and 308 W in their logs, and the "not a boost burst" warning from the MAMF boost check all come from that idle GPU. MAMF-finder's TFLOP/s do not depend on telemetry. On MI300X it reads 750 W and 1,315 MHz sustained and 2,096 MHz at boost, matching the 750 W cap in note 9 of Stas Bekman's table.
- Power cap on MI350X (`amd-smi static --limit`, job 453520): the socket power limit is 1,000 W, equal to the maximum limit and to the brochure's maximum TBP. During a sustained bf16 4096x4096x16384 matmul in JAX (job 453523), the GPU held 1,000 W at a 70-73 °C hotspot, below the 100 °C slowdown temperature, and its 8 compute dies ran at 1,332-1,513 MHz, about 1,400 MHz on average. At 1,400 MHz the peak formula (256 CUs x 4,096 bf16 FLOPs per clock) gives about 1,470 TFLOP/s, 64% of the 2.2 GHz figure. Against that power-limited peak, MSMF is about 86%, JAX by kernel time on the same shape (1,189 in job 454577) about 81%, and JAX by untraced wall clock in job 453523 (1,145 TFLOP/s) 78%. MAMF's short bursts may run above the sustained clock before the GPU reaches its power limit, so the 1,400 MHz figure does not bound MAMF.
- With torch imported, the `amdsmi` Python binding from `/opt/rocm-7.2.0` reports no GPUs, because torch has already loaded the ROCm SDK's own `libamd_smi.so.27`. `setup_envs.sh` uses the SDK's binding instead.
- Next: measure a training step with `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` to see whether the faster hipBLASLt kernels for the k and v GEMMs carry over. Separately, check whether XLA can use the rocBLAS solutions TunableOp picked for 4608x4096x7168 and 2048x4096x4096 (`tunableop-*.csv` in the results directory), and whether those solutions close the remaining gaps.

</details>

Edit: first posted with JAX numbers from node k007-004 while MAMF-finder ran on k007-002. All MI350X numbers now come from k007-002. JAX medians now use the true median of the ten windows. The MI350X telemetry note was corrected after jobs 453520 and 453523 showed MAMF-finder sampling a different GPU. Second edit: JAX now reports kernel time from a `rocprofv3` trace next to wall clock, and comparisons with MAMF and MSMF use kernel time (jobs 454577-454580). This corrects the earlier reading that the wall-clock gap came from XLA's kernel choice; XLA's choice still costs 17-33% on the k and v shapes, where it picks its own Triton GEMM. The Snowball shapes now cover separate k and v projections, the k and v weight gradients and the input gradients, and the paragraph names every projection behind a shared shape. Added the Triton-off comparison, the run-to-run variation note, and the TunableOp library choices. Scripts moved to `experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/`, and the grid arguments are now `--m-range`, `--n-range` and `--k-range`.

### MI350X Triton `ragged_dot` rewrite and tuning: batch 64 step 2.634 → 2.426 s, 8.58% → 9.32% MFU

Commit: 8471641 (local, not pushed) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 453565 (A/B), 453564 (microbenchmark), baseline 453384

PR: #9859 (AMD Instinct only; NVIDIA, TPU and megablox unchanged).

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" \

  --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 --compilation-cache-dir $WORK/jax-cache --batch-size 64
```

| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.426 s (was 2.634) | 108,100 (was 99,500) | 9.32% (was 8.58%) | 184.2 GiB (unchanged) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- Loss matches the baseline to 4 decimals (11.7770 vs 11.7769 at step 19).
- Forward and dlhs now launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a device-side tile map, instead of a full row grid per expert. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. drhs uses an explicit flat grid. Rows past the last group are zero-filled.
- Tuned for MI350X: 256×256×64 tiles, 8 warps, 2 stages for forward and dlhs; 256×128×64, 4 warps, 1 stage for drhs; plus chiplet-aware program order. Blackwell, TPU and megablox are unchanged.
- Per call on one GPU at batch 64 (M=131072), before → after TFLOP/s:

  | Layout | w13 | w2 |
  |---|---|---|
  | fwd | 583 → 722 | 555 → 667 |
  | dlhs | 554 → 760 | 538 → 757 |
  | drhs | 410 → 581 | 396 → 573 |

  A dense `jnp.matmul` of the same FLOPs runs at about 925–958; XLA fp16 `ragged_dot` at 24–98. At batch 8 the forward pass goes from 2.27 ms to 0.36 ms. Jobs 453500 and 453564.
- At batch 64 the tile map alone changes nothing. With the old blocks, w13 forward takes 2.95 ms either way. The gain there is block tuning. At batch 8 the tile map is a 4.6× win.
- `plgpu.CompilerParams` exposes only `num_warps` and `num_stages`, so AMD knobs (`waves_per_eu`, `matrix_instr_nonkdim`, `kpack`) can't be set from Pallas.
- drhs, at 573–581 TFLOP/s, is the remaining gap. Both of its operands are contraction-strided.

</details>

RCCL uses 112 channels, ring and the Simple protocol. The model's async EP all-gathers take 4.1 ms (about 280 GB/s) because they share compute units and HBM with concurrent compute: next to a matmul, an all-gather hides only 42% of it, even with the latency-hiding scheduler on.

The other 120 ms is async EP traffic not hidden by compute. The `msccl` f32 all-reduce kernels take under 2 ms.
- Pooled-wave moves about half the bytes of ring, but XLA leaves 130 of its 156 all-to-alls per step synchronous on the main stream with none of their time overlapped, and they launch 64 workgroups against 112. Exposed time is 402 ms. It also drops more assignments: 5.4% against ring's 0.9% at capacity factor 1.0.
- Against the old kernel (2.634 s), `save_moe` on the new kernel is 11.3% faster.

🤖 Matmul-alone time in the MI350X `--overlap` runs (jobs 453572, 453633, 453651) takes one of two values between runs: about 2.46 ms in `min64`, `ring`, `prio-on` and `lhs-prio-off`, and about 2.88 ms in the other 16. Details: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9886#issuecomment-6047294744

Because the variance is between processes, re-timing the matmul inside a run does not remove it. To compare settings, run each setting in several processes, interleave them, and compare medians of a per-run ratio such as the hidden fraction `(t_collective + t_matmul − t_both) / min(t_collective, t_matmul)`, using the matmul-alone time of the same run.

PR: #9880 (draft, merge after #9860). `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` comes from #9852.

```bash
JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.580 s | 165,900 | 14.31% | 206.5 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What it does.** `ring` all-gathers every token to all 8 GPUs and reduce-scatters a full-size output, but with top-4 of 256 experts a token reaches only 3.3 GPUs on average. `ring_dedup` (new module `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring_dedup.py`) sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`, plus a small `all_to_all` of per-row combine weights and local expert ids. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule, grouped layout and Triton `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32 and returns one row per token. All hidden-width movement is a gather (ring's `_dispatch_rows`/`_combine_rows`), so there are no scatter-adds in either pass.
- **Sender capacity** is `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing (0.416 × 32,768 per GPU). At 1.1 it sends 537 MB per collective per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring's all-gather or reduce-scatter (46%), and drops no tokens at the sender in these runs.
- **A/B, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile cache per job, `JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`, median of steps 2-19:**

  | Base | Remat | ring | `ring_dedup` | Jobs |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | merged (gather combine + Triton routing top-k) | recompute_all | 1.798 s, 12.57% | 1.688 s, 13.40% (-6.1%) | 454022, 454026 |
  | merged | save_moe | 1.730 s, 13.07% | 1.580 s, 14.31% (-8.7%) | 454012, 454021 |
  | before the gather combine | recompute_all | 1.865 s, 12.13% | 1.735 s, 13.03% (-7.0%) | 453921, 453922 |
  | before the gather combine | save_moe | 1.842 s, 12.28% | 1.637 s, 13.81% (-11.1%) | 453960, 453968 |

  The two changes stack partly. With `save_moe`, the gather combine alone saves 112 ms, `ring_dedup` alone 205 ms, both together 262 ms. Peak memory changes by at most 0.7 GiB. Step-19 loss is within 8e-4 of ring in every pair. The drop rate is 1.00% vs 0.99% (`recompute_all`) and 1.12% vs 0.93% (`save_moe`).
- **Numerics.** f32 CPU unit tests on 8 shards match ring and a dense reference to 1e-5 in value and in gradients for x, combine weights and both expert weights, including a forced sender-drop case. At full shapes in bf16 on MI350X, one layer differs from ring by 0.2-0.5% relative in value and gradients. That comes from ring's bf16 summation; `ring_dedup` sums in f32.
- **Profile (steps 10-12, GPU 0, ms per profiled step, ring vs `ring_dedup`, both before the gather combine).** `recompute_all`: large EP collectives take 481 vs 311, exposed collective time is 357 vs 288, and MoE dispatch/combine kernels take 150 vs 42. `save_moe`: 386 vs 211, 402 vs 266, and 147 vs 40. Each large `all_to_all` takes 1.6-2.7 ms, against 3.3-4.2 ms for ring's collectives.
- **What is still exposed:** the forward return and backward dy `all_to_all`s are synchronous (about 60 ms each per step), and the small metadata `all_to_all`s take 0.8-0.9 ms per call under `save_moe`, where they queue behind the large transfers.
- The latency-hiding scheduler gave 1.594 s vs 1.637 s before the merge, but 1.591 s vs 1.580 s after it (job 454027), so leave it off.
- One run (454010) hit the step-5 GPU-7 out-of-memory on a 96.6 GiB allocation, the same failure seen at batch 96 in job 453660, and hung. The retry (454021) ran clean. Since diagnosed as allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer and fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` (#9901).
- **Follow-ups:** packing the metadata into the activation rows and chunking the expert MLP were tried and did not help; see the next comment. Not tested on TPU or NVIDIA.

</details>

comments.author: asartran
comments.body:
### ring_dedup follow-ups: packing routing metadata into the dispatch rows is bit-exact but step-neutral; chunking the expert MLP does not pay

Commit: 8e2de3e7e5 (packing), c68890bc53 (token chunks, not proposed) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 454468, 454469 (base); 454499, 454662 (pack); 454596, 454674 (chunks); 454563, 454665, 454574, 454692, 454700 (pack + chunks); 454628, 454699 (pack + latency-hiding scheduler)

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 --compilation-cache-dir <fresh dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode <mode> [--moe-token-chunks 2]
```

| Variant | Remat | Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ring_dedup (base) | save_moe | 1.586 s | 165.3k | 14.26% | 206.5 GiB |
| + metadata in rows | save_moe | 1.588 s | 165.1k | 14.24% | 206.4 GiB |
| + token chunks 2 | save_moe | 1.623 s | 161.5k | 13.93% | 206.4 GiB |
| + token chunks 2, latency-hiding scheduler | save_moe | 1.602 s | 163.6k | 14.11% | 207.8 GiB |
| ring_dedup (base) | recompute_all | 1.709 s | 153.4k | 13.23% | 158.1 GiB |
| + metadata in rows | recompute_all | 1.710 s | 153.3k | 13.22% | 157.4 GiB |
| + token chunks 2 | recompute_all | 1.752 s | 149.6k | 12.90% | 157.4 GiB |
| + metadata in rows, latency-hiding scheduler | recompute_all | 1.678 s | 156.2k | 13.48% | 160.0 GiB |
| + token chunks 2, latency-hiding scheduler | recompute_all | 1.668 s | 157.2k | 13.55% | 160.0 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- Every run compiled cold into its own cache directory (step 0 at 322-329 s). Step is the median of steps 2-19. Run-to-run spread is about 1.5%: a repeat of "metadata in rows, recompute_all" gave 1.742 s, then 1.710 s.
- Metadata in rows: the combine weights (f32 bits), local expert ids (int16) and the sender count ride in 16 extra bf16 columns of the dispatch all-to-all, and a custom VJP returns the combine-weight gradients in the backward dx all-to-all. One layer at batch-64 shapes gives bit-identical outputs and gradients against the current ring_dedup, with 4 all-to-alls instead of 6. The full model does not get faster: profiled steps drop 60 ms, but the profiler adds about 0.3 ms per collective call, and the backward dx all-to-all becomes synchronous.
- Token chunks: each shard runs dispatch, expert MLP and return per token chunk. With the default GPU schedule, every all-to-all done follows its start with no GEMM in between, so nothing overlaps and chunking is 1.5-2.5% slower. With the latency-hiding scheduler, the transfers do overlap the other chunk's GEMMs, but half-size `ragged_dot` calls take 13% longer (332 -> 375 ms per profiled step), which cancels the gain. Without drops, chunked outputs and dx match exactly; per-chunk receiver capacity doubles receiver drops at capacity 1.0 (0.08% -> 0.15% in one layer). Not proposed.
- The latency-hiding scheduler now helps ring_dedup with recompute_all by about 2% (1.709 -> 1.668-1.678 s). save_moe without it is still fastest.
- Loss at step 19 matches base within 2e-4 in every run; drop rates are 1.0-1.2%.
- Two of 19 full-model runs hit the known step-3 single ~97 GiB allocation failure and hung; the retries ran clean. This is the allocator fragmentation fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` (#9901).
- Next: overlap the synchronous forward return and backward dy all-to-alls (about 55 ms each per profiled step) with work that does not shrink the GEMMs, such as the shared-expert MLP backward.

</details>

comments.author: asartran
comments.body:
### One gradient all-reduce per weight after the layer scan: works, keeps gradients, no speedup on MI350X

Commit: bd8e11a · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Job: 453915 (on 60b253d), 454011 (on 67ca557)

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash --remat-mode <recompute_all|save_moe>
```

| Base | Remat | Variant | Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 60b253d | recompute_all | baseline | 1.844 s | 142,200 | 12.26% | 158.4 GiB |
| 60b253d | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.852 s | 141,600 | 12.21% | 158.4 GiB |
| 60b253d | save_moe | baseline | 1.824 s | 143,700 | 12.39% | 205.8 GiB |
| 60b253d | save_moe | deferred reduction | 1.856 s | 141,200 | 12.18% | 205.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | recompute_all | baseline | 1.786 s | 146,800 | 12.66% | 157.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.786 s | 146,800 | 12.66% | 157.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | save_moe | baseline | 1.748 s | 150,000 | 12.94% | 205.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | save_moe | deferred reduction | 1.741 s | 150,600 | 12.99% | 205.9 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- What the in-scan all-reduces are: on this mesh (`expert=8`, other axes 1), every non-expert block weight is replicated across the batch. Explicit sharding types each layer's weight gradient as replicated, so the backward while body all-reduces it per layer. Per layer that is 5 gradient all-reduces: q/k/v/gate and w_o in the attention `cond` branch, one combined GatedNorm/router/shared w_gate/w_up, shared w_down, and the two RMSNorm weights. The forward body adds one router-stats all-reduce, for 6 × 26 = 156 per step. XLA's combiner can't merge across loop iterations or `cond` branches.
- The change: weights that only feed matmuls are marked `reduced` over the batch axes before the scan (`levanter.grug.sharding.defer_batch_grad_reduction`). Their gradients leave the scan unreduced and are all-reduced once per stacked weight. FSDP-sharded leaves (`data` > 1) are left unchanged. RMSNorm weights keep the per-layer reduction. Stored parameter shardings don't change.
- Gradients match. On CPU (tiny preset, f32, 8 devices) the loss and 26 of 27 leaves are bit-identical. On GPU (medium preset, bf16, job 454079) the loss is identical, and baseline-vs-change errors (at most 0.63% relative L2) equal baseline-vs-baseline. The full-model losses match too.
- The backward loop goes from 5 gradient all-reduces per layer to 1, but the step doesn't get faster. In a profiled A/B (job 453987) the change saves 43 ms per step, but the profiler adds about 0.3 ms to every collective call. Unprofiled, the 130 removed calls cost about 11 ms, and the single 2 GB all-reduce after the scan takes about 16 ms on the main stream. The bytes are the same either way, and the per-layer calls were bandwidth-bound, not latency-bound.
- Not proposing a PR for MI350X. Small collectives should be priced from unprofiled step times, not from trace durations.

</details>

comments.author: asartran
comments.body:
### Hiding `ring_dedup`'s synchronous all-to-alls behind the shared expert: no gain

Commit: 3838b71 (local, on the `ring_dedup` base 91286fc) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 454847, 454872, 454943 (overlap + latency-hiding scheduler); 454865, 454945, 454949 (latency-hiding scheduler only); 454857, 454892 (baseline)

```bash
JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton \
  XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Variant (`save_moe`) | Step | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1.589 s | 14.23% | 206.5 GiB |
| latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s (best 1.569) | 14.36% | 207.7 GiB |
| shared expert pinned under the transfers + latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s | 14.36% | 208.2 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What was tried.** A `custom_vjp` around `ring_dedup`'s return `all_to_all` runs the shared-expert MLP between the transfer's start and its use. The backward does the same for the dy `all_to_all` and the shared-expert backward. Ordering is enforced with `optimization_barrier`. The shared expert moves into the backend (`moe_mlp(..., shared_expert=...)`). f32 CPU tests on 8 shards match `ring_dedup` plus a separately computed shared expert to 1e-5 in value and in every gradient.
- **The forward return was already hidden.** In the default schedule the forward return `all_to_all` is async and spans the shared-expert forward GEMMs (30 of 45 ms per profiled step run under it). The synchronous forward transfer is the dispatch. The backward dy `all_to_all` is synchronous.
- **Without the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers backfire.** XLA's default GPU schedule doesn't move all-to-all starts earlier, so it placed the shared GEMMs before the start and every large `all_to_all` became synchronous: 1.610 s vs 1.589 s (+1.3%).
- **With the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers work, but the time just moves.** Unhidden ms per profiled step with the scheduler, before → after pinning:

  | Transfer | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | dy | 41 | 26 |
  | dx | 7 | 33 |
  | forward return | 66 | 90 |

  The scheduler was already hiding dx behind the shared backward. It won't split that work across dy and dx, and scheduling-group annotations, which could force the split, crash the compiler on this ROCm build.
- **`recompute_all`:** baseline 1.707 s, scheduler only 1.695 s, scheduler + pinning 1.703 s.
- **The latency-hiding scheduler alone** gives -0.9% (`save_moe`) and -0.7% (`recompute_all`) here, but an earlier run measured +0.7%. That's within run-to-run noise (about 1.5%), so the defaults stay as they are.
- **Next:** profile-guided latency-hiding scheduling (`xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`), so the scheduler fills windows by measured transfer time; or find other independent work for the forward dispatch window.

</details>

comments.author: asartran
comments.body:
### Re-baseline on `main` (#9832, #9830, #9777) and `ragged_all_to_all` on MI350X: ring numbers unchanged; ragged runs only through XLA's decomposer, 55x slower

Commit: d733cb2 (local: the `ring_dedup` base 91286fc merged with `main` at e11ab28) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 455320, 455339, 455394, 455439, 455430 (re-baseline); 455374, 455386, 455429, 455437 (`ragged_all_to_all`); 455319, 455338 (collective probe); 455382 (tests)

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl <ring|ring_dedup|ragged_all_to_all> [--pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1] --remat-mode <save_moe|recompute_all>
# ragged_all_to_all additionally: XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_unsupported_enable_ragged_all_to_all_decomposer=true
```

| Backend | Remat | Batch | Step | MFU | Peak mem | Drops | Before merge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ring | save_moe | 64 | 1.730 s | 13.07% | 206.0 GiB | 1.01% | 1.730 s |
| ring_dedup (transport 1.1) | save_moe | 64 | 1.582 s | 14.29% | 206.5 GiB | 1.15% | 1.580 s |
| ring | recompute_all | 64 | 1.768 / 1.773 s | 12.78% | 158.0 GiB | 0.96% | 1.798 s |
| ring_dedup (transport 1.1) | recompute_all | 64 | 1.691 s | 13.37% | 158.2 GiB | 0.97% | 1.688 s |
| ragged_all_to_all + decomposer | save_moe | 64 | OOM (534.6 GiB temp) | | | | |
| ragged_all_to_all + decomposer | recompute_all | 16 | OOM (158.2 GiB temp) | | | | |
| ragged_all_to_all + decomposer | recompute_all | 8 | 23.302 s | 0.12% | 190.0 GiB | 6.55% | |
| ring | recompute_all | 8 | 0.420 s | 6.73% | 147.6 GiB | 4.50% | |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **`ring` and `ring_dedup` don't move.** `main` changed no code on their path; its library changes are in `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py`, `sonic.py` and a new `topk.py`. `ring` with `recompute_all` came out 1.5% faster in two runs, which is at the edge of run-to-run noise.
- **FLOPs per example are unchanged at 6.52e13** (5,305,917,440 per token, 7 full-attention layers, from the benchmark's own log). #9633 was already in the base, so every earlier MFU stands.
- **`ragged_all_to_all` without extra flags** fails with `UNIMPLEMENTED: Device communicator is not implementing`, as on MI300X. The backend's `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true` is not a flag in JAX 0.11.0's XLA, so passing it aborts the process. Symmetric buffers, the one-shot kernel flag and every `xla_gpu_ragged_all_to_all_mode` value still return `UNIMPLEMENTED`. The ROCm plugin contains a ragged all-to-all device kernel, but no flag in this build routes the op to it.
- **The decomposer works but is far too slow.** `--xla_gpu_unsupported_enable_ragged_all_to_all_decomposer=true` gives correct results; a single 10.7 MB-per-GPU transfer takes 13.6 ms. In the full model it is 55x slower than ring at batch 8 and runs out of memory at batch 16 and 64. Loss matches ring at batch 8 (11.7922 vs 11.7921 at step 19).
- **#9832's Triton kernels don't run on ROCm.** They go through `jax_triton`, which is only in the CUDA `gpu` extra, so the backend falls back to gathers and zero-filled buffers.
- **#9777 works:** no more `gfx950` parse error. The QuACK path is skipped and `ragged_dot` is used.
- **#9830's routing top-k** used `jax_triton` and served only the hero model, while the June model used #9889's ROCm-only Pallas top-k. #9942 now replaces both with one Pallas-Triton kernel that runs on NVIDIA and AMD: within 1% of #9830's kernel at the hero shape on GB200, and 1.4-3.3x faster than #9889's at the June shape.
- **Tests** (`test_grugformer_moe.py`, single process): 80 passed, 16 skipped, 5 failed. The 5 are the `ragged_all_to_all` tests, which now fail with `UNIMPLEMENTED` instead of the `gfx950` parse error. With the decomposer, 16 of the 17 ragged tests pass. The remaining `test_ragged_moe_reads_no_unwritten_transport_rows_on_gpu` failure turned out to be a test artifact that also reproduces on 8x H100, not a backend bug. Don't export `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton` for this file: its CPU-subprocess tests inherit it and fail.
- `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` from `main` worked unchanged.

</details>

issues.title: [grug] Raise Snowball MFU on AMD Instinct GPUs

issues.author: gonzalobenegas
issues.body:
## TL;DR

The expanded GLM-5.3/Pi collection is complete: 1,310 attempts, exactly five for each of 262 tasks, with 1,285 native reward vectors and 25 ungraded attempts. The first SFT baseline will use all available solver traces, including partial-credit, zero-credit, truncated, and interrupted traces, without reward or completion filtering. Native Pi sessions exist for 1,251 attempts; 39 further attempts have raw model-request captures only, and 20 startup failures have no model requests. The initial 30-attempt Pi batch is separate and remains in scope. Collection artifacts are preserved and no owned sandboxes remain. The agreed first run starts from September 21 Datakit SFT, uses biology traces only, peak LR 1e-4, three epochs, 131,072-token sequences, and effective batch 16. Save/export only the final model. Full-parameter SFT uses fresh AdamH, 3% warmup, cosine decay to 1e-5, and frozen router biases. Evaluate BixBench first; broader evaluations are deferred until that result. Preparation is complete: 5,120 reconstructed windows, 73,894,261 assistant target tokens per epoch, and 960 optimizer steps for three epochs. CoreWeave 32 H100s is selected. CPU optimizer/checkpoint tests and full lint/type checks pass. Cache construction is running. The CPU training coordinator is submitted and waits for verified cache completion before requesting the selected 32 H100s; no optimizer updates have run.

## Description

Use the existing [Skill2Env Harbor release](https://hub.harborframework.com/datasets/skill2env/skill2env) to collect GLM-5.3 demonstrations for Snowball. This issue owns task selection, rollout collection, SFT, and the before/after experiment. [#9630](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9630) owns Skill2Env Atlas intake; [#9258](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258) owns biology evaluation coverage and protocols.

Start with biology tasks, prioritizing biological data analysis relevant to BixBench. If the usable pool is too small, consider a separately recorded expansion to general scientific data analysis and statistics. Keep relay methods, where a teacher takes over from student-generated actions, for a later experiment.

### Candidate data

The October 5 metadata inspection covered all 7,496 tasks in release revision 2, version `1.0.1`, with content digest `sha256:bef4f739bde8d865af04c04a2cb1c84ecad83b52dd558f4d582dd46c7933666c`. The 268 candidates are a source-skill and description-based shortlist, not an exhaustive taxonomy or a validated training pool.

| Candidate category | Tasks | Source-skill identifiers |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Genomics and single-cell analysis | 95 | 40 |
| Proteins and structure | 49 | 16 |
| Chemistry and drug discovery | 45 | 22 |
| Biomedical data and lab workflows | 79 | 28 |
| Total | 268 | 106 |

Examples include paired airway RNA-seq analysis with PyDESeq2, sparse CELLxGENE summaries, Scanpy PBMC QC and clustering, DepMap dependency analysis, and pysam BAM/VCF processing. Different skill identifiers can cover related workflows; 106 identifiers do not establish 106 independent task families. Many released tasks repair pipelines against offline fixtures. Their usefulness for BixBench remains a hypothesis.

Skill2Env's [source attribution table](https://github.com/NVlabs/Skill2Env/blob/507eab4d9952968de2be98f8729d3c66d487285a/SkillHub/skillhub_source_licenses.csv) includes K-Dense scientific skills and AlterLab academic skills. Preserve task-specific source and license records when selecting data or sharing traces. The selection rule below preserves this initial shortlist independently of temporary local files.

### Pilot sequence

1. Review candidate instructions, environments, and graders. Six initial tasks passed reference/no-op controls. The user authorized direct collection on the other 262 metadata-selected candidates; those tasks have not passed additional controls. Review grader validity when interpreting scores; it is not a selection gate for the unfiltered baseline. Record any grader defects; the existing Atlas assessment found a grader defect in a separate three-task sample.
2. Freeze the task manifest and evaluation split. Group related tasks and shared-data variants when defining development and held-out sets. BixBench-overlap checking is not a prerequisite for this collection, as decided on October 5; preserve task provenance.
3. Pin the Snowball starting checkpoint, tokenizer, training recipe, agent harness, and evaluation settings. Run a small end-to-end collection and formatting check before expanding collection. Record compute budgets before launching sandbox or training work.
4. Generate GLM-5.3 trajectories. The initial collection finished five attempts per task on the six control-checked tasks, for 30 attempted rollouts. The expanded collection targets five attempts for each of the other 262 tasks, for 1,310 new attempts. Preserve every attempt, raw conversations, tool outputs, exact model settings, task revisions, and the full native reward vector; keep incomplete and ungraded outcomes separate. Inspect component-score distributions, solution diversity, and token volume. The first SFT baseline uses all available solver traces without reward or completion filtering. Preserve interrupted prefixes and record conversion or recovery gaps without manufacturing missing content. Rewards are graded; do not reduce them to binary success or require all components to equal 1 by default. Native executable rewards do not reproduce the paper's additional rubric-scoring layer.
5. Prepare all available solver traces for the first SFT baseline; the earlier 200–500 selected-trace target is superseded. Report attempted, complete, graded, and selected traces; component-score distributions; unique tasks and task families; total tokens; and supervised assistant tokens. Size the first SFT run from those observations; the target is a planning budget, not a proven minimum. Prioritize coverage of distinct tasks when expanding collection. Additional attempts on one task do not increase task diversity.
6. Train with loss on assistant turns, preserving user and tool messages as context. Evaluate the final checkpoint against the unchanged Snowball parent on the fixed BixBench protocol using the same Pi harness and budgets. Decide on broader evaluations after reviewing BixBench. Keep infrastructure failures separate from incorrect answers.

Recent Snowball work motivates a bounded test: a [5,000-conversation GLM continuation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9719) regressed on several benchmarks, while [other agent SFT mixtures](https://gist.github.com/lukedhlee/8669f5b6f97e4e3bae72344a8fd51f4b) improved agent benchmarks. Neither establishes a BixBench benefit from this dataset.

### Agreed SFT settings

| Setting | Selected value |
| --- | --- |
| Parent | `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21`; revision `b8c07f7df1df65525abbfdbcd1572318ba11c42f` and native tokenizer/template pinned |
| Data | All available GLM/Pi biology solver traces; no reward or completion filter; no general SFT or pretraining replay |
| Run count and peak LR | One run at `1e-4` |
| Duration | Three epochs |
| Training sequence length | 131,072 tokens; verify actual lengths with the parent tokenizer |
| Effective global batch | 16 sequences per optimizer update; accumulation as needed |
| Parameter updates | Full-parameter SFT; imported router biases frozen, router weights and other model weights trained |
| Optimizer | Fresh AdamH; beta1 0.9, beta2 0.95, epsilon 1e-8, weight decay 0, gradient clipping 1.0 |
| Schedule | 3% warmup, then cosine decay from 1e-4 to 1e-5 over the run |
| Checkpoints | Final model save/export only; no intermediate or per-epoch checkpoints |
| Initial evaluation | Parent and final model on BixBench with identical Pi harness and budgets; broader evaluations deferred until that result |

The nominal batch is 2,097,152 token positions per update, matching 64 × 32,768 in [the teacher-only reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9582). Masking, padding, and sequence construction determine actual supervised tokens. Three epochs and peak LR 1e-4 follow that precedent; its reported evaluations use final checkpoints, and its intermediate checkpoint cadence is undocumented. The final-only saving decision avoids repeated serialization and storage of this model.

Use reconstructed conversations with each actual assistant output supervised once, carried context masked, and interrupted outputs left without invented termination markers. The finalized dataset has 5,120 windows at length 131,072, 320 steps per epoch, and 960 steps total. Target four CoreWeave nodes with eight H100s each. BixBench comparison uses `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` (205 tasks), Pi, one attempt per task, 32,768 context / 8,192 output, and matched grading. The CPU training coordinator is submitted; GPU training remains gated on cache verification.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Unfiltered GLM-5.3 demonstrations of biological analysis improve Snowball's held-out BixBench accuracy under the same harness and execution budget. Measure paired BixBench changes and uncertainty, task coverage, tool-format failures, and response lengths. Broader evaluation is deferred until the BixBench result. Review trace completeness, native grades, and sequence handling before training; preserve negative results.

comments.body:
🤖 SFT planning: the collected biology traces are large enough for a bounded specialist experiment, but selected volume and transfer remain unmeasured. No training launch is part of this plan.

At the 13:49 UTC collection snapshot, 488 normal-ending traces had every native component at 1. Structural checks leave 482 candidates over 156 tasks, with 20,017,782 provider-counted output tokens. This includes reasoning and possibly auxiliary compaction output; it is not the unique Snowball-supervised token count. The larger normal-ending pool also contains partial-credit trajectories. Preserve their component vectors and decide acceptance after grader review. Repeated rollouts add solution variants without adding independent tasks.

Relevant precedents:

- [Snowball agent SFT #9225](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9225#issuecomment-5753734747): OpenThoughts-Agent plus instruction-following data improved pooled SWE-bench from 14.5% to 24.1%, with weaker Terminal-Bench results. The [recorded recipe](https://gist.github.com/lukedhlee/d152f86a58e8619a988361e1502f9e55) used full-parameter AdamH, LR 1e-4, betas 0.9/0.95, epsilon 1e-8, clip 1, zero weight decay, 3% warmup, 32,768-token sequences, and batch 64. Its second epoch added no SWE-bench gain.
- [Recent Snowball relay continuation](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-acont-step999): 8,982 traces, LR 3e-4, three passes, and batch 16 at 65,536 tokens; reported SWE-bench 45.3%, versus 13.8% for September 21. This starts from an already relay-trained parent, and the author flags possible confounders. It is evidence that thousands of agent traces can matter, not a matched biology recipe.
- [The exact Skill2Env paper, section 5.4](https://github.com/NVlabs/Skill2Env/blob/main/paper/Skill2Env_arXiv.pdf): GLM-5.3 assistant-token SFT at 128k gave weak or negative Qwen results. [Snowball expert negatives #9719](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9719) also include a regressing 5,000-conversation GLM continuation. Data quality, formatting, dose, and parent choice need measurement.

Proposed recipe, pending parent selection and token accounting:

- Parent: recommend the shared September 21 Datakit SFT checkpoint; pin weights, tokenizer, and its own thinking/tool chat template together. The parent is not yet fixed.
- Data: review high-scoring complete traces first; allow partial credit through an explicit component-based policy. Exclude malformed, looping, interrupted, or grader-invalid candidates from the initial training pool. Balance task families and deduplicate near-identical solutions. Hold out 10–15% of task families before sequence construction; all repetitions and segments of a task stay in one split.
- Targets: preserve main-agent reasoning, tool calls, final answers, and end-of-turn tokens; mask system/user/tool observations. Render GLM/Pi messages in Snowball's native format. Count each assistant target once. Keep auxiliary compaction generation outside the initial target set and preserve its resulting summary when it is part of the actual solver context.
- Training: full-parameter fine-tuning with fresh Adam state; betas 0.9/0.95, epsilon 1e-8, clip 1, weight decay 0, BF16 compute, frozen router bias. Start at LR 1e-5 with 5% warmup and cosine decay to 1e-6. These LR and warmup choices are conservative proposals, not a previously successful biology setting. A later 3e-5 arm can test sensitivity.
- Budget: one pass initially, save at approximately quarter/half/full exposure; extend to two passes only if held-out behavior improves. Target 65,536-token examples and effective batch 16, subject to memory validation. Inspect target coverage before finalizing length. Long traces require context-preserving examples at valid turn or compaction boundaries; do not silently truncate them. Use separate examples until the selected implementation proves packed-document isolation. Derive steps from the actual sequence cache, not provider usage totals.

Replay is an ablation. The [September 21 parent card](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21) records 20% long-context pretraining replay, but that does not establish the required fraction for this short continuation. Compare biology-only with 80% biology / 20% audited general SFT replay, at equal biology-token exposure and the same optimizer/schedule. Use token-based allocation and log both processed and loss-bearing tokens. General replay should cover reasoning, instruction following, and compatible tool use. Raw pretraining replay would be a separate arm with full next-token loss; it is most useful to test if broad or long-context retention regresses.

Before training: freeze the parent, audit graders and target formatting, compute unique target and context-token counts with Snowball's tokenizer, then validate one update, checkpoint export, and Pi tool-call parsing. Evaluate parent and selected intermediate checkpoints with identical Pi budgets on biology development tasks and BixBench, plus instruction-following, code/math, and long-context retention checks. Use development results for tuning and reserve the final benchmark comparison. GPU allocation and spend remain to be specified after sequence accounting.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Heads-up from marin#9920: the HF export in this recipe will fail at the final step unless patched.

`train.py` sets `model_ref` to the regional S3 copy of the parent (`ctx.artifact_path(parent)`), and `train_lm` passes that through as the converter's `reference_checkpoint`. The HF export hook calls `save_pretrained` without `save_reference_code`, which resolves to True for Snowball because `GrugMoeHfConfig` is not a `transformers` class. `_save_code_local` then calls raw `hf_hub_download(repo_id="s3://...")` and raises `HFValidationError` before the config, tokenizer and shard index are written. We hit exactly this on 2026-10-07 at 23:57 UTC in a CruxEval SFT run with the same recipe (marin#9920).

Since this run exports only once (`hf_save_steps=steps + 1`) with native checkpoints disabled (`save_interval=None`, `save_final_checkpoint=False`), a 960-step run would end with nothing saved. Fixes under discussion in #9920: plumb `save_reference_code=False` through `AdaptorExportConfig` → `save_hf_checkpoint_callback` → `save_pretrained` (the parent repo has no code files, so nothing is lost), or make `_save_code_local` URL-aware like the load paths.

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 Reproduced two Grug streaming-parser defects against the pinned vLLM source and submitted matched two-question checks with a tested fix.

1. The parser can interpret an earlier assistant turn's end-think marker as closing the new turn's reasoning. This exposes new reasoning as ordinary text.
2. When a response starts with a tool call and no think markers, the reasoning parser returns text but does not transition to the tool-parsing phase. Hermes never receives the call.

The CPU regression suite uses the actual pinned parser source with a minimal tokenizer vocabulary fixture, including combined Grug/Hermes streaming with fragmented tool-call chunks. A separate method-level reproduction used the pinned tokenizer. These tests do not replay full model output. Baseline: **4 failed, 7 passed**. Fix: **11 passed**, both as a native patch and as a plugin over unchanged source. The plugin is currently local at `experiments/sft/skill2env_bio/grug_turn_parser.py`; it is not committed or upstreamed yet.

The checks use the standard evaluation runner, pinned Pi policy, Grug/Hermes, 32,768 context, 8,192 output, and identical settings for both models. Only the reasoning-parser plugin changes. Both inference jobs are running and have loaded their weights:

- SFT: `/exedev/eval-20261008-155004-skill2env-bio-9775-final-policy-parserfix-check-1fe9`
- Parent: `/exedev/eval-20261008-155018-skill2env-bio-9775-parent-policy-parserfix-check-f603`

A closer look at the previous overflow shows Pi **did compact** first: its estimated post-compaction context was 15,566 tokens, but the next request exceeded the server's budget. The compaction summary also contained leaked reasoning. The server reports **at least** 24,577 input tokens, not an exact prompt length. Published Pi 1.1.0's overflow detector recognizes that error; why this trace did not retry compaction remains unresolved. We keep the budget unchanged while checking whether the parser repair removes the failure.

Evidence bundle (tests, patch/plugin, reproduction, compaction events, configs, submission receipts): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/teacher-traces/skill2env-bio-sft-20261006/parser-fix-evidence-20261008.tar.gz`.

Next gate is correct tool execution and trace handling, not a positive reward on these questions. Then run the full matched evaluation and inspect before/after traces for improved, regressed, and unchanged questions.

**Live-check update, 16:04 UTC:** the SFT check completed, but it does not pass the correctness gate. Q1 executed 7 tools and Q2 executed 6, then both ended with tool-call blocks in the reasoning field. Neither had a Harbor exception; both received reward 0. These remaining outputs require raw-token inspection to distinguish malformed generation from parser handling; the CPU tests alone do not establish that distinction.

Parent Q1 also received reward 0 and ended with `ContextLengthExceededError` after 7 tool results. Its trace confirms that an earlier overflow **did** trigger compaction and a successful retry; a later overflow ended the task. Parent Q2 is still running, currently installing R packages. The running sandbox confirms Pi, pi-ai, and pi-agent-core are all version 1.1.0. Full evaluation remains unlaunched.

🤖 Both bounded comparison batches finished. All 40 short-prompt requests and six real BixBench attempts have saved results. Both inference servers stopped normally; none of the six trial sandboxes remain.

### Real BixBench question

`bix-18-q1` asks for mean circularity of the P. aeruginosa genotype with the largest mean area. One attempt per model and harness, no retries:

| Harness | Parent grade | Biology SFT grade |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Pi, thinking on | 0 | 0 |
| Pi, thinking off | 0 | 1 |
| mini-swe-agent, thinking on | 1 | 1 |

All six attempts graded without infrastructure exceptions or timeouts. Both parent Pi attempts and SFT Pi thinking-on produced zero tool results. Parent mini-swe-agent completed nine tool results; SFT completed thirteen under Pi thinking-off and eleven under mini-swe-agent. Both mini-swe-agent runs ended with native `Submitted` status. The successful SFT Pi run wrote the notebook and answer artifacts and reported Wildtype mean circularity 0.0760.

This establishes that both checkpoints can solve this real task under mini-swe-agent, and SFT can solve it under Pi with thinking off. One question and one attempt per condition do not establish general benchmark performance.

### Controlled short-prompt check

Each checkpoint received the same brief prompt asking it to start by calling bash to read a CSV, ten times per thinking setting (temperature 0.7, seeds 0–9). No tool was executed in this check. A valid response means a parsed bash tool call with JSON arguments containing a string command.

| Setting | Parent valid tool calls | Biology SFT valid tool calls |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Thinking on | 10/10 | 3/10 |
| Thinking off | 10/10 | 10/10 |

Raw decoded streaming output was matched to all forty response IDs. All seven SFT thinking-on failures placed tool blocks inside unclosed reasoning. Each had only 195 prompt tokens and generated 25–66 tokens, with finish reason `stop`, not `length`. These failures therefore do not require long context or exhausting a token limit. The SFT Pi thinking-on BixBench attempt showed the same pattern at 1,651 input / 27 output tokens.

Four SFT thinking-off outputs also contained unclosed reasoning markers with tool blocks, although the API returned valid tools. Disabling thinking changes how these outputs are handled; it does not demonstrate that generation itself is repaired. The exact training or serialization cause remains unproven.

### Protocol and evidence

Both models used 32,768 context / 8,192 output, the same Grug reasoning and Hermes tool parsers, Pi 1.1.0 or mini-swe-agent 2.1.0, and Harbor `0985d012bcf4cc9d1acb1a831a86350cd31ac72a`. The task came from `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3`, with 300-second agent and verifier limits. It was selected using a prior correct GLM-5.3 / Terminus-2 attempt taking 18.68 agent seconds; that historical timing is only a selection heuristic.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
Task curation now declares environments by their package needs (an Environment with pypi pins or a uv lock, apt packages and data downloads) and runs those without an image as locked-down local subprocesses on the worker. TaskSpecs exported for such tasks carry a packages lock reference instead of a docker image. rolloutengine's grading path still requires an image for any non-empty environment requirements; it should build the same uv environment from the lock and grade in a local sandbox, as the curation worker does.

Part of #9798.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`lower_task` rejects shell grading without a digest-pinned image, and `_machine_spec` maps every image-free environment to ShellSim. The local backend in #9936 accepts `HostImage` and an already-built virtual environment, while #9798 still builds that environment inside task curation and exports an image reference for local graders. The packages-lock TaskSpec shape described here is not in either current PR head, so the fix crosses the persisted task contract, environment provisioning, and rollout grading.

**Relevant code**
- [`lowering.py#L53-L74`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3c94c2e78b07d67b1db524add9f696d1115506ee/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/lowering.py#L53-L74) — image-only shell validation.
- [`machines.py#L55-L66`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3c94c2e78b07d67b1db524add9f696d1115506ee/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/machines.py#L55-L66) — image or ShellSim selection.
- [`machine.py#L367-L440`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ad8b242034037811a793d6f38e256b1af591376f/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/machine.py#L367-L440) — local factory and supported specs.
- [`grader_environment.py#L45-L103`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/experiments/post_training/task_curation/grader_environment.py#L45-L103) — curation's locked uv builder.
- [`environment.py#L18-L24`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/convert/environment.py#L18-L24) — current local grader export.

# Lock-based local grading

## Design

1. Land the #9798 TaskSpec environment contract first. A local grader must carry an immutable lock reference and digest, Python version, and its apt/data requirements (or a reference to a pinned manifest containing them). Validate that the selected backend supports every requirement before acquiring a machine. A lock URI alone cannot reproduce apt packages or data downloads.
2. Move the uv materialization path out of `experiments/post_training/task_curation/grader_environment.py` into shared library code used by curation and rolloutengine. Resolve and verify the lock, build a cache entry keyed by the complete environment identity, install with `uv pip sync --require-hashes`, and publish a completion marker only after a successful build. Preserve the existing cross-process build lock and retry an incomplete entry.
3. Let rolloutengine select `HostImage` plus the resolved virtual environment's bin directory for a lock-based grader, while retaining `RegistryImage` for image requirements and ShellSim for an empty environment. Remove the unconditional image check in `lower_task`; require the local backend and `NetworkPolicy.DENY` for the lock path. Keep this path limited to trusted grader scripts that inspect model output. Graders that execute submitted programs need the stronger sandbox selected by curation, since #9936 explicitly treats local commands as trusted.
4. Make unsupported apt/data needs a preflight error until the worker can satisfy their pinned manifest. Do not silently grade with missing packages or data. Keep environment build failure distinct from a scored task failure.

## Testing

Use a tiny local lock and trusted shell grader to exercise TaskSpec serialization, lowering, environment build, grading, and cleanup end to end. Cover a wrong lock digest, an interrupted cache build, unsupported apt/data needs, and rejection of a lock-based grader on an image-only backend. Run the rolloutengine and taskcompendium default suites, plus the local Shellbox backend tests; verify an existing image grader still takes the image path.

## Open question

Should the exported lock reference point to a complete pinned environment manifest, or should TaskSpec carry the Python, apt, and data fields directly? Settle this in #9798 before implementing the shared resolver; both curation and rolloutengine must interpret the same persisted contract.

spillover_issues.body:

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The combined command uses the root pytest config, which leaves `pytest-asyncio` in strict mode; TaskCompendium's package config uses auto mode. Its 18 unmarked async test functions fail before execution (the first after 94 passes). Zephyr also chooses a regional GCS bucket for temporary shards in pipeline tests; one test timed out after 60 seconds and passed in 3.5 seconds with a local `MARIN_PREFIX`.

**Relevant code**
- [`pyproject.toml#L523-L550`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/pyproject.toml#L523-L550) - root pytest settings
- [`lib/taskcompendium/pyproject.toml#L24-L25`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/lib/taskcompendium/pyproject.toml#L24-L25) - package async mode
- [`test_convert_executable.py#L236`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/lib/taskcompendium/tests/test_convert_executable.py#L236) - first failing async test
- [`zephyr/context.py#L276-L277`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/context.py#L276-L277) - remote temporary storage default

# Proposed Fix

Mark TaskCompendium's async tests explicitly and give its tests a per-test local `MARIN_PREFIX`. These changes keep the root pytest mode unchanged and keep test shards off GCS. With equivalent command-line settings, the combined suite passed 889 tests and skipped 9 in 46.81 seconds on `a95cc117e2`; I will send a focused PR against #9798's branch.

spillover_issues.author: muchanem
spillover_issues.body:
`ShellSimMachine.run` lets a shellsim simulator panic propagate as a `SimulationError` instead of returning a failed `Result`. A model-chosen shell command can therefore abort a whole rollout trial rather than producing a non-zero exit the agent can react to.

Reproduction (shellsim 0.1.29 via `lib/shellbox`'s `shellsim` extra): pipe a file into a Python one-liner that consumes stdin through a generator expression.

```
cat /workspace/numbers.txt | python3 -c 'import sys; print(sum(int(l) for l in sys.stdin))'
```

raises

```
SimulationError: shellsim operation panicked: internal error: entered unreachable code: generator execution cannot suspend (src/python/vm/iteration.rs:1074)
```

The same program reading `< /workspace/numbers.txt`, using `open()`, or using a list comprehension over piped stdin runs fine, so the trigger is a generator expression consuming piped stdin. The generator case itself is a shellsim defect (rjpower/shellsim); this issue is about shellbox's handling: `Machine.run` for the ShellSim backend should convert a simulator panic into a `Result` with a non-zero exit and the panic text on stderr (or a typed `MachineTerminated`), the way a real shell surfaces a crashed interpreter, so one bad command does not take down the trial.

Seen in Taskforge's live validation round on ShellSim, where an adversary trial came back ungraded because its first shell command hit this.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

ShellSim 0.1.29 raises `SimulationError` for the reported piped-stdin generator; the simulator accepts a subsequent command. `_run_source()` lets the exception escape through both `ShellSimMachine.run()` and the agent's persistent `ShellSimShellSession.execute()`, aborting the trial.

**Relevant code**
- [`machine.py#L45-L55`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/shellsim/machine.py#L45-L55) - agent shell result conversion
- [`machine.py#L96-L134`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/shellsim/machine.py#L96-L134) - simulator call and verifier result
- [`agent.py#L130-L142`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/agent.py#L130-L142) - tool response path

# Proposed Fix

`BashAgent.run()` calls `ShellSimShellSession.execute()`, while Harbor verification calls `ShellSimMachine.run()`; both reach `_run_source()` and currently propagate the panic. Catch `shellsim.SimulationError` at each public command boundary and return a completed, non-zero result with the diagnostic in stderr or shell output, respecting the caller's output limit. Add regression coverage for both paths and a successful follow-up command.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
The TaskTrove math converters in experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/tasktrove/math.py grade with verifiers that call sympy's sympify on model text. sympify evaluates arbitrary expressions, so a crafted reply can hang or exhaust the grader. The graders now run as locked-down worker subprocesses with rlimits, which bounds the damage, but the parsers should use parse_expr with a restricted transformation set or verifyit's math mode instead.

Part of #9798.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

PR #9798 accepts two SHA-256-pinned TaskTrove math scorers and stages each archived `tests/verifier.py` unchanged. Both accepted revisions call `sympify` on reply-derived scalar text; the prism revision passes `evaluate=False`, which does not remove the eval-based parser. The worker's limits bound a failed grade, but [SymPy warns that `sympify`](https://docs.sympy.org/latest/tutorials/intro-tutorial/basic_operations.html#converting-strings-to-sympy-expressions) and [`parse_expr`](https://docs.sympy.org/latest/modules/parsing.html#sympy.parsing.sympy_parser.parse_expr) use `eval` on unsanitized input.

**Relevant code**
- [`math.py#L48-L57`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/tasktrove/math.py#L48-L57) - Accepted scorer hashes.
- [`math.py#L138-L177`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/tasktrove/math.py#L138-L177) - Archived scorer staging.
- [`math_gym.tar.gz`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/experiments/post_training/task_curation/tests/fixtures/math_gym.tar.gz) and [`math_prism.tar.gz`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/experiments/post_training/task_curation/tests/fixtures/math_prism.tar.gz) - Both verifier revisions.

# Proposed Fix

`MathConverter.__call__` validates the archive hash, packages its scorer, and `tests/test.sh` runs `_scalar()` on the model reply. In #9798, retain the hash guard but stage a repository-owned replacement for these two known scorer revisions: parse Python-style scalar syntax with a bounded AST allowlist of numeric literals, symbols, arithmetic, and required math functions, then construct SymPy expressions without evaluating arbitrary Python; keep the existing LaTeX path and typed comparison rules. Reject calls outside the function allowlist, attributes, subscripts, and oversized expressions before constructing expressions. Add harmless code-shaped submissions that must score zero, plus positive and negative cases for scalar, set, interval, tuple/list, and equation grading through both archive fixtures; run the five TaskTrove math sources' sample verification before #9798 merges. Restricted `parse_expr` transformations alone would retain its documented `eval` behavior.
