spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
Task-curation declarations can give a grader an `Environment` with only a pypi lock (`GRADER_PACKAGES`). The pipeline places such graders in a bubblewrap sandbox on the Zephyr worker, over a self-contained Python environment built from the lock (`experiments/post_training/task_curation/environment_runtime.py`). The exported TaskSpec carries `packages_lock` and no `docker_image`.

RolloutEngine cannot grade those tasks today. `_machine_spec` in `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/machines.py` builds a `ShellSimBuiltins` source whenever `docker_image` is absent, and `require_environment_source` then rejects it, so passing the curation controls does not show that the task can be graded during rollouts.

Proposed fix: move the lock-driven environment builder (`LocalRuntime`, `LocalGraderMachines`) out of the experiment into a runtime both the pipeline's controls and RolloutEngine share, below `rolloutengine` in the dependency order (taskcompendium or shellbox). `_machine_spec` then selects shellbox's local backend with `HostImage` and the built root for lock-only environments, and an image with gVisor or Iris otherwise. Exercise the complete path on a supported backend.

Raised in the review of #9798.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The exported task from #9798 records `packages_lock` but no image. RolloutEngine selects `ShellSimBuiltins` for that environment, then shared grading rejects the machine because a lock-only grader requires the local backend's `HostImage`. The builder that supplies that backend lives under the experiment and reads its artifact type, so RolloutEngine cannot reuse it without crossing the package dependency boundary.

**Relevant code**
- [`pipeline.py#L122-L141`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/42fcc4d0ee5f550a297fc89cea510faaea88fb2e/experiments/post_training/task_curation/pipeline.py#L122-L141) — exports the lock-only environment.
- [`machines.py#L53-L68`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/42fcc4d0ee5f550a297fc89cea510faaea88fb2e/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/machines.py#L53-L68) — selects `ShellSimBuiltins` without an image.
- [`shell.py#L73-L79`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/42fcc4d0ee5f550a297fc89cea510faaea88fb2e/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/shell.py#L73-L79) — accepts `HostImage` for local grading.
- [`environment_runtime.py#L44-L170`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/42fcc4d0ee5f550a297fc89cea510faaea88fb2e/experiments/post_training/task_curation/environment_runtime.py#L44-L170) — builds and mounts the lock environment.
- [`machine.py#L348-L392`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/42fcc4d0ee5f550a297fc89cea510faaea88fb2e/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/machine.py#L348-L392) — local factory requires `HostImage` and rejects resource allocations.

# Proposed Fix

This change should follow #9798, which is still open and owns the curation runtime. A separate implementation PR against current `main` would duplicate its code.

## Design

1. Put the lock runtime in `taskcompendium.runtime`, below RolloutEngine in the dependency graph. Move `LocalRuntime` and `LocalGraderMachines` there, using shellbox's `build_python_environment` and `LocalMachineFactory`. Keep artifact construction in the curation experiment. The shared runtime must not import `marin` or `experiments`.
2. Make the exported `EnvironmentRequirements` self-contained for local grading: retain `packages_lock` and add the lock SHA-256 and declared data names from the built artifact. The shared runtime checks the downloaded lock against that digest and keys its completed root by the lock, data, Python version, and runtime package contents. The curation driver and RolloutEngine then call the same builder for the same task.
3. Select a verifier factory per grader environment in RolloutEngine, since one backend name can refer to several lock roots. For a lock-only grader on `Backend.LOCAL`, build the root and pass `HostImage`, the mounted bin directory, and `NetworkPolicy.DENY` into the existing bounded grading lifecycle. Keep the image path on its selected image backend. Validate backend compatibility and reject local CPU, memory, storage, or GPU allocations before starting a rollout; shellbox's local backend cannot enforce them.

## Testing

Write the failing rollout regression first. Use an exported lock-only TaskSpec and a real bubblewrap local factory on a supported Linux runner; grade a correct and an incorrect submission, check that the grader cannot access the network, and verify machine cleanup. Keep a focused test for image-backed grading. The existing local backend tests skip when bubblewrap is unavailable, so the full-path test needs a CI runner where bubblewrap is guaranteed.

## Cost and open question

The first local grade may build CPython and packages on the host; the cache must be content checked, and the grading sandbox remains network denied. Which existing CI runner can guarantee the bubblewrap capabilities and uv downloads needed for the full-path regression?

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
An Iris retry can reuse an evaluation's serialized `EvaluationIdentity.run_id` and `output_dir`. The replayed Evalchemy process then appends samples and overwrites `record.json` under an already sealed result URI. A tracker link can therefore change its score after it has been sealed.

Reproduce:
1. Submit an evaluation batch through `experiments/evaluation/launch.py` and let an Evalchemy process finish and seal its FineStore archive.
2. Cause Iris to classify the parent task or Evalchemy child task as retryable after that write, such as a post-completion `PodDeleted` or worker preemption.
3. Observe that the replay has a new Iris attempt or child-job ID but writes to the original FineStore path and run-level `record.json`.
4. Compare the first completed attempt, replayed attempt, and current record at that URI.

Expected: an Iris retry must preserve completed results as immutable artifacts. It should either skip a successfully sealed evaluation or allocate attempt-specific run IDs and output paths. A later failed attempt must not downgrade or replace an earlier succeeded record.

Confirmed examples:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261003-210313-Aleph-Alpha-Kolibri-1-mbppplus-b75b/results` first completed at 262/378 (`0.6931216931`). A parent-task retry ran a second MBPP+ child against a new serving endpoint and wrote 274/378 (`0.7248677249`) to the same path. The current `record.json` and FineStore view report the second score.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261002-002728-laion-snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203-gpqa-diamond-5b7b/results` changed from `0.636` to `0.5993265993` after a parent `WORKER_FAILED` retry replayed GPQA-Diamond against a new serving child.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-nupa-9a91/results` held a sealed 5,000-item attempt with 2,414 correct answers (`0.4828`). Iris classified the completed Evalchemy child attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted`, retried the same task and path, and the final canonical record became `0.4788`.
- The Kolibri retry also changed MATH500 from `0.984` to `0.992` and HumanEval+ from `0.774` to `0.7682926829` under unchanged result URIs. When the retried parent was later killed, several earlier succeeded Kolibri `record.json` files were rewritten as `infra_failed`.

`_run_id()` is evaluated while constructing the batch in `experiments/evaluation/launch.py`; Iris retries replay the serialized batch. `write_record()` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py` then writes unconditionally to `{prefix}/{run_id}/record.json`.

comments.body:
🤖 Trinity Mini NUPA provides a child-task-level reproduction and rules out partial aggregation.

The Iris child `/benfeuer/eval-20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-a679/eval-nupa-cb8a6a13/0` has three attempts:

- Attempt 0 completed on 2026-10-02 at 06:24:54 UTC, then Iris recorded `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted` and scheduled a retry.
- Attempt 1 wrote and sealed a complete 5,000-item `NUPA5K-Loose` archive. The archive had 4,510 scored responses, 490 classified infrastructure failures, and 2,414 correct answers, so the recovered score was 2,414 / 5,000 = `0.4828`. The tracker sealed that complete attempt on 2026-10-03.
- Iris again recorded the attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` and started attempt 2 at 2026-10-03 10:41:20 UTC. Attempt 2 completed successfully on 2026-10-04 at 15:46:05 UTC and wrote `0.4788` to the same result URI.

Both reported scores cover the full 5,000-item panel. The difference is between complete replays of one stochastic evaluation under one run ID, not between a partial and final aggregate.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`build_evaluation_batch()` serializes one `run_id` and results path per evaluation. An Iris replay enters the same runner with that identity; the evaluator can reopen the sealed archive, and `write_record()` overwrites the canonical record. The September 27 and October 6 incidents document successful records replaced by retry or cancellation failures.

**Relevant code**
- [`launch.py#L213-L220`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/launch.py#L213-L220) — serializes the run ID and results path
- [`runner.py#L243-L269`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L243-L269) — reuses the path and writes a record
- [`records.py#L319-L325`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L319-L325) — replaces `record.json`
- [`store.py#L175-L181`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py#L175-L181) — reopening clears the seal

# Attempt isolation and first-success publication

[PR #9813](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9813) already changes evaluation scheduling and uses `StepSpec` status to skip successful steps on restart. Its own description identifies the remaining crash window between writing a record and marking the step successful. This plan belongs in that PR or its successor; a separate runner PR would overlap it.

## Design

Keep the launch `run_id` as the stable tracker identity. Allocate a fresh attempt ID when an evaluation actually starts, and write Evalchemy or Harbor output, its FineStore archive, and an attempt record under `{records_prefix}/{run_id}/attempts/{attempt_id}/`. Pass that attempt's results path to the executor, so a retry cannot reopen an earlier sealed archive. Preserve the attempt ID and Iris job IDs in the attempt record for audit.

Publish `{records_prefix}/{run_id}/record.json` only after an attempt's output is sealed and its metrics are validated. Use a storage-conditional update (GCS generation or S3 ETag/create precondition) so the first successful record wins even if a lock expires or two writers race. Failure records may replace an earlier failure while no success exists; after success, later attempts cannot replace the canonical record or its referenced results. A replay that finds a canonical success should return that record path before starting serving or evaluation, including when a previous worker died after publication but before `StepSpec` wrote `SUCCESS`.

Update the launcher, runner, record writer, reporting path, and EvalDash reader together. Existing run pages keep the stable `run_id`; the canonical record points at an immutable attempt's results. Keep old flat-layout records readable for historical runs. A deliberate new evaluation gets a new launch `run_id` instead of changing an existing score.

## Costs and risks

The additional attempt directory and conditional publication path change the persistent layout and require both CoreWeave S3 and GCS semantics to be exercised. Step status and record publication can disagree after a crash; recovery must treat a canonical success as complete. Existing readers that assume results live directly under `{run_id}/results` need updating.

## Testing and completion

Add a regression that publishes a successful, sealed attempt, interrupts before step success, then replays the batch: no new evaluator runs and the canonical record and seal remain byte-for-byte unchanged. Cover failure-then-success, success-then-failure, and two competing publishers; verify that attempt records remain separate and EvalDash keeps the first successful score. Run the repository's local evaluation tests and pre-commit checks, then exercise conditional publication on the configured S3 and GCS backends before landing.

## Open question

Should the canonical path show the latest failed attempt until a success arrives, or should failed attempts appear only in the attempt history? The first option preserves current failed-run visibility; either choice must prevent a failure from replacing success.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
We implemented eleven model-merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 Snowball 67B A2B checkpoint variants with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores. Sequential merging via selective expert transfer retained almost all of the NUPA source's performance and matched the BFCL source's score, but the three best merges retained essentially none of the Base model's routed experts. We have not yet run the complete cohort of policy evals needed to judge non-targeted performance.

[Earlier RLVR experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735) showed that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can strongly and unpredictably affect non-targeted benchmarks. It can introduce or repair behavioral defects that change scores while leaving the model's underlying “knowledge” essentially untouched. For example, a model might return every numeric answer, such as “31.7,” as “final_answer.31.7” instead of the requested “Final Answer: 31.7,” collapsing a benchmark score. We conservatively treat these as model defects to remedy under normal use conditions rather than grader defects to smooth. Each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats, so we investigated efficient ways to combine checkpoints.

Model merging is popular among hobbyists and is rumored to be used extensively at frontier labs, though the scientific literature is thin. Most merging methods use very few FLOPs and often require no GPUs. This makes merging relevant to our goal of reaching the frontier quickly and FLOP-efficiently.

The target Snowball checkpoint had largely improved but acquired two severe behavioral defects that sharply reduced NUPA and BFCL performance. We used two other Snowball models as merge sources. Each was an expert on one target benchmark, but both were generally inferior to the target, or Base, model. The objective was to raise performance on both disparate target benchmarks without degrading non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all standard merging approaches we tried failed to raise both target scores strongly. They restored capability weakly on both benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. Extensive experimentation led us to try sequential merging via selective expert transfer. It retained performance on both targets, but required discarding essentially all Base parameters from the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

These three merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched the source BFCL score. None appears to meet the objective of avoiding degradation on non-targeted benchmarks; we will reserve judgment until the complete policy eval cohort has run.

Sequential merging via selective expert transfer appears promising for complex MoE merges. Our best strategy combined weights from the NUPA, BFCL, and Base models:

1. Start with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template.
2. Replace selected NUPA routed experts with BFCL experts. In each layer, select 32 expert positions using BFCL activation measurements and copy BFCL weights into them. This discards all Base routed experts.
3. Change NUPA's shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We made three versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

The percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version had the highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model:

- Starting with BFCL, copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts yielded only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA, copying 32 BFCL-selected experts yielded 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor, the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We found no better joint result with those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights, and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce. This was likely an unusually difficult merge target because tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently:

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA's tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base's tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers. This affects benchmarks even with unchanged weights: the same input text can produce different token IDs, and the same output token ID can decode to different text. The numerical vocabulary did not change. Both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

The chat templates also formatted tool use differently:

- NUPA's template presents tool definitions as one JSON array; Base's presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA's template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided; Base's omits those IDs.
- The templates differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Using the other template changes the model input and therefore the benchmarks. In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input:

| Model weights | With Base configuration and tokenizer | With NUPA configuration and tokenizer |
|---|---:|---:|
| NUPA, with no expert transfer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 17.07% BFCL-Parity |
| NUPA, with 16 BFCL experts per layer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 21.14% BFCL-Parity |

In another ablation, restoring NUPA's own special-token rows increased NUPA200 from 29.00% to 39.00%. These rows represent control tokens, such as message boundaries.

The agent's experimental design was flawed and needs a follow-up study. It drifted almost immediately from adding specialist capabilities to Base toward combining the two specialists. We will enforce that specialist changes target only a small, measured fraction of Base weights in the follow-up study, and may also control for the tokenizer confound.

---

Figure 1. Retrospective comparison of 113 evaluated checkpoint variants across 11 method families. Each bar sums the NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity percentage scores of one checkpoint (range 0–200); its two segments are the two benchmark scores. Left: best observed sum in each family. Right: best observed sum in the chronological prefix that fits a common 1.0e15 estimated merge-FLOP budget per family. Trials are ordered by first evaluation submission; shared calibration and precursor exports are charged once within each family, including precursor exports from other families. No later trial is skipped ahead of an over-budget trial. Experiment counts: Serial merging 28; Activation-guided transfer 21; Layer / component merging 30; Expert Merging++ adaptation 4; Weighted averaging 5; DARE-linear 2; OTA + FFG adaptation 4; RAM / RAM+ 4; Task arithmetic 10; TIES 3; DARE-TIES 2. The 21 activation-transfer variants include five random-transfer and five recipient/metadata controls; these ten controls consume budget but are excluded from maxima in both panels. Counts represent checkpoint variants with both scores, not independent seeds or all attempted jobs. The campaign largely combined the NUPA and BFCL specialists; the best serial checkpoint copied about 0.76% of all parameter values unchanged from Base, the intended recipient model. Unequal search effort and differences in tokenizer and model configuration files between checkpoints confound algorithm comparisons. Both benchmarks were optimization targets; these maxima do not establish held-out gains or general capability retention. Compute is an arithmetic estimate, not measured hardware FLOPs or total search cost: evaluation, original benchmark captures, NUPA activation collection, failed attempts, I/O and quadratic attention work are excluded. The full recorded BFCL replay corpus is charged once as shared setup to each family that uses activation-selected transfers; that replay alone costs about 3.8e16 FLOPs, so activation-dependent trials exceed the main-panel budget even with those omissions. The right panel is a retrospective budget filter over the observed trial sequence, not a prospective equal-compute experiment.

[Budget sensitivity](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/resolve/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/plots/method-shootout/budget_sensitivity.png) · [Per-family scores](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/plots/method-shootout/family_ranking.csv) · [Per-experiment data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/plots/method-shootout/experiment_data.csv) · [Plot source](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/plots/method-shootout/plot_shootout.py)

Only Shared100 exceeds the historical BFCL specialist score; Shared075 and Shared050–Attention025 remain below it. These are not matched reruns.

Shared050–Attention025 combines equal NUPA/Base shared-expert weights with 75% NUPA and 25% Base attention-component weights, on top of the selected BFCL expert transfer; it differs from the shared-only 50% variant. [Exact recipe](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/recipes/serial-bfcl032-shared050-attention025-step12.json). Provenance percentages count all stored scalar parameter positions by recipe source: “pure” means copied from that parent, and “blended” means multiple source contributions. They do not measure active parameters or token allocation. In Shared100, the remaining attention, router, embedding, and output-head weights come from NUPA. Blended variants can contain Base contributions even when their pure-Base count is zero.

The metadata ablation swapped the loading/input-preparation file bundle, including tokenizer and chat-template files; it does not isolate individual tokenizer, template, or configuration effects. The 29.00% to 39.00% NUPA200 comparison restored NUPA's native special-token embedding/output rows in a NUPA-weight recipient that previously preserved Base's rows. The [introduction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975)'s response-behavior explanation is a working hypothesis; these experiments do not establish that internal knowledge was unchanged.

Broad capability retention is already in doubt: Shared100 scored 89.80% MATH500 and 52.19% GPQA-Diamond, versus the historical Base references of 95.00% and 67.30%; see the [recorded sentinel scores](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/TRACKER.md). “Sealed” means this merge-search campaign is complete. It does not imply that the full policy evaluation cohort was completed or that follow-up work is ruled out.

🤖

# Implemented merging methods

This catalog covers eleven method families implemented in Marin for the Grug/Snowball 67B campaign; coefficient, density, layer-count, and donor-choice sweeps are configurations within these families. Metadata/tokenizer and special-token-row controls are part of checkpoint construction, not additional merging algorithms. An anchor is the starting checkpoint, donors supply weights or updates, and the recipient is the checkpoint receiving transferred experts; Step92 denotes Snowball Mixed-RLVR, Step12 denotes Grug Antidoom-RLVR1, and Step20 denotes Grug Reference-KL, with exact source revisions preserved in each recipe.

Costs are approximate **arithmetic FLOPs per output checkpoint**, estimated from the implementation with `P = 6.7e10` stored parameters, usually two donors plus an anchor, and approximately `2.0e9` active parameters per token during calibration. A multiply-add counts as two FLOPs; comparisons/top-k selection, random-number generation, casts, hashing, storage traffic, and quadratic attention work are excluded, so these are operation-count estimates rather than hardware-profiler measurements.

Wall-clock figures are rounded **observed Iris task durations for representative runs**, including task setup, checkpoint reads, and output writes, but excluding queueing, benchmark evaluation, hyperparameter search, and Hugging Face publication. These timings are not controlled hardware-throughput comparisons: ordinary exports used 16–32 CPU cores; learned calibration and moment collection used eight H100s per job, and their CPU export stages are included explicitly below.

1. **Weighted averaging.** We form a convex combination of aligned parent weights in FP32 and cast the result back to the checkpoint dtype, following the weight-averaging approach of [Model soups (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.05482). With two donors and an anchor, our implementation costs approximately **`3.4e11` FLOPs (`5P`) per merge** and took **34 minutes** for `avg-050-025-025`.

2. **Task arithmetic and delta amplification.** We subtract an anchor from each donor and add scaled donor updates back to the anchor, including the amplified-update sweeps described by [Task Arithmetic (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04089). The two-donor implementation costs approximately **`5.4e11` FLOPs (`8P`) per merge** and took **34 minutes** for `task-075-075`, with coefficient amplification leaving the arithmetic count unchanged.

3. **TIES merging.** We retain the largest-magnitude updates within each tensor, elect their weighted sign, and average sign-consistent updates using retained coefficient mass, adapting [TIES-Merging (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708) with tensor-local pruning. This costs approximately **`1.3e12` arithmetic FLOPs (`19P`) per merge**, excluding top-k comparisons, and took **85–87 minutes** for the 20% and 80% density configurations.

4. **DARE-linear.** We randomly drop task-vector coordinates, rescale surviving updates by inverse retention probability, and add them to the anchor, following [DARE (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03099). The dense masked implementation costs approximately **`8.0e11` FLOPs (`12P`) per merge**, excluding random-number generation, and took **48–49 minutes** at 20% and 80% retention.

5. **DARE-TIES.** We apply DARE dropping/rescaling before TIES sign election and sign-consistent aggregation, combining [DARE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03099) with [TIES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708). This costs approximately **`1.4e12` FLOPs (`21P`) per merge** and took **49–51 minutes** at 20% and 80% retention, because the implementation still processes dense tensors after masking.

6. **Structured layer and component merging.** We assign tensor-specific coefficients to early/late layers, depth ramps, attention, routed experts, shared experts, routers, normalizations, or output heads, including exact donor replacements through the [campaign checkpoint merger](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/lib/marin/src/marin/merging/checkpoint.py). Our two-donor code evaluates the dense weighted expression even for zero/one coefficients, costing approximately **`3.4e11` FLOPs per merge**, with **33 minutes** observed for the `direct-router-step20` representative.

7. **Activation-guided individual-expert transfer.** We favor routed experts used frequently on the target benchmark and infrequently on the other benchmark, then copy or blend their rows while preserving the recipient router, with matched-size random transfers as controls in the [campaign selector](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/select_experts.py). With an existing selection, transferring 16–64 of 256 experts per layer costs approximately **`3.6e11–4.2e11` FLOPs per merge**, with **41–43 minutes** observed for the 16/32-expert exports; the reusable BFCL tool-use replay alone adds approximately **`3.8e16` FLOPs across four separate eight-H100 jobs lasting 4–7 minutes each (about 22 summed job-minutes)**, excluding original benchmark captures and NUPA numeric-response activation collection, so this is not a complete fresh-selection setup cost.

8. **Serial merging.** We materialize an intermediate merge and apply another merge to it, including the top recipe by NUPA200 plus BFCL-Parity percentage-point sum: Step20 routed-expert transfer followed by Step12 shared-expert replacement, as specified in the [winning recipe](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/recipes/serial-bfcl032-shared-step12-100.json). That two-stage construction costs approximately **`7.1e11` FLOPs and 80 minutes per final checkpoint** when both stages are built afresh, or **`3.4e11` FLOPs and 38 minutes** for its second stage when the intermediate already exists, excluding reusable expert selection.

9. **RAM and RAM+.** We classify task-vector coordinates as active when their absolute update exceeds a threshold in one or multiple donors, retain unique updates, average shared updates, and optionally amplify unique contributions using the tensor-local `ramplus_tl` rule from [RAM (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13572) and [mergekit](https://github.com/arcee-ai/mergekit/blob/main/docs/merge_methods.md). Both variants execute approximately **`1.1e12` FLOPs (`16P`) per merge** in our implementation, with **53 minutes** observed for `ram-eps1e4` and **49 minutes** for `ramplus-r010-cap020`.

10. **Behavior-trained coefficients: Expert Merging++ adaptation.** We first learn layer/component coefficients for routed experts, shared experts, attention, and routers, then split flattened weight tensors into importance-allocated contiguous chunks and refine their coefficients to match domain-specific parent hidden states and logits before static export, adapting [Expert Merging / Expert Merging++ (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25712) to native GrugMoE. With 48 calibration examples and 24 warmup plus 96 chunk-training steps, the estimate is approximately **`3.0e14` FLOPs and 7 hours 50 minutes per merge** for `expertpp-hidden`, comprising **7 hours 4 minutes on eight H100s plus 46 minutes of CPU export**, with approximately **`4.0e11` FLOPs** attributable to export alone.

11. **Curvature-aware merging: Optimization Trajectory Aware (OTA) with calibrated tensor-local Fast Fisher Grafting (FFG).** We use square roots of calibrated squared response-loss gradients to weight donor updates and retain coordinates by squared-update-times-moment saliency within each tensor, adapting [OTA + FFG (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11167) because original optimizer moments were unavailable. A fresh two-donor calibration plus the `ota-ffg-d050` export costs approximately **`6.0e13` FLOPs and 3 hours 20 minutes per merge**, comprising **98 minutes of sequential eight-H100 moment collection plus 102 minutes of CPU merging**, while reusing the moments reduces each additional merge to approximately **`1.3e12` FLOPs and 102 minutes**.

The static estimates count the operations actually executed, including coefficient-zero passes; sparsity therefore does not imply proportional FLOP savings. GPU estimates use `2AT` for forward passes and `6AT` for forward/backward passes, where `A` is active parameters per token and `T` is processed tokens, plus full-weight coefficient mixing or moment accumulation: the learned example used 5,233 teacher tokens and 12,936 student tokens, while the two curvature collectors used approximately 4,175 tokens in total.

Evidence: [cost inputs and formulas](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/records/method-cost-inputs.json), [recorded Iris durations](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/records/method-timings/index.json), [arithmetic implementation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/lib/marin/src/marin/merging/arithmetic.py), [calibration implementation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/calibrate.py), and [campaign results](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/TRACKER.md).

The archived recipes preserve historical source revisions and storage paths. Private storage URLs are provenance only; use the public parent checkpoints and your own output locations. Full benchmark-capture replay is unavailable for the reasons in the [reproducibility statement](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/REPRODUCIBILITY.md).

The experiment set is sealed. This issue records the completed campaign; it does not claim that the merges preserve performance outside the two optimization targets. The cleaned PR consolidates the reusable Marin implementation; the historical source links preserve the code revisions used to obtain the reported measurements.

Parent checkpoints: [Base](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02/tree/50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e), [NUPA](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab), and [BFCL](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04/tree/fd07ef0f2b78a83099a0042e59c00de986e7b647).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 Archived the description before automated prose cleanup.
<!-- marin-prose-cleanup-archive:4bfd869fcdae98c533af6be0a74388e9b287e84bc8d831082c50fd06ef41ece2 -->

<details><summary>Original description</summary>

```markdown
What we did: Implemented eleven different model merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 checkpoint variants on Snowball 67B A2B with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores.

Why we did it: We observed in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735 that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can have strong and unpredictable effects on non-targeted benchmarks; the reason for this is that it can introduce or repair behavioral pathologies which can radically alter benchmark scores while leaving the underlying model "knowledge" essentially untouched. 

e.g., after RLVR, a model might start outputting every numeric answer such as "31.7" in a corrupted format like "final_answer.31.7" instead of the task's requested "Final Answer: 31.7", resulting in a complete collapse in a benchmark score.

Since we do not want our model to behave pathologically under normal use conditions, we conservatively treat these as model defects to be remedied rather than a benchmark grader defect to be smoothed.  The question, then, is how to remediate such defects most efficiently when each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats at the same time.

Model merging is a popular technique among hobbyists, and there are rumors it is used extensively at frontier labs, but the scientific literature has always been a bit thin. What is unquestionably true is that most model merging methods are extremely FLOP-efficient, in many cases not even requiring GPUs. Since we want to reach the frontier quickly *and* FLOP-efficiently, it would be irresponsible of us not to take a serious look at model merging.

Results: Our target in this case was a Snowball checkpoint which had largely improved but had acquired two severe behavioral defects causing its performance on NUPA and BFCL to degrade dramatically. We used as merge sources two other Snowball models, each of which was an "expert" on one of these benchmarks, but both of which were generally inferior to the student. The merge objective, then, was narrow and challenging; (1) *boost* target model performance on two disparate benchmarks while (2) *avoiding degradation* on non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all of the standard model merging approaches we tried failed at (1) -- the typical pattern was that merging either restored capability weakly on both target benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. After extensive experimentation, we postulated that *sequential merging via selective expert transfer* might retain performance on both benchmarks, and this turned out to be the case, but at a significant cost; we had to discard *essentially all of the parameters from the base model* in the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

Our three most successful merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched source BFCL score, accomplishing (1); but none of these three merges appear to have accomplished (2), and it would be surprising if they did. We will, however, reserve final judgment on this until we have run the complete cohort of policy evals on these checkpoints.

COMMENT: Sequential merging via selective expert transfer is a promising approach for complex MoE merges.

Our most successful strategy used weights from three models to build one model: NUPA, BFCL, folding into Base.

1. We started with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template (more on this later).
2. We then replaced selected routed experts in NUPA with BFCL experts. In each layer, we selected 32 expert positions from BFCL activation measurements and copied the BFCL weights into those positions. *All of the Base routed experts were discarded*.
3. Finally, we changed the NUPA shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We built three separate versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

These percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version produced our highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because the experiments showed that its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model --

- Starting with BFCL: copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts into it gave only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA: copying 32 BFCL-selected experts into it gave 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most of its numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor: the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We did not find a better joint result through those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce.

COMMENT: This was very likely an unusally difficult merge target because our tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

* The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently.

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA’s tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base’s tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers.

This matters for benchmarks, even when the weights are unchanged. The same input text can produce different token IDs. The same output token ID can also decode to different text.

The numerical vocabulary did not change. For example, both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

2. The chat templates formatted tool use differently.

- NUPA’s template presents tool definitions as one JSON array. Base’s template presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA’s template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided. Base’s template omits those IDs.
- The templates also differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Thus, “use the other template” changes the actual input to the model (and therefore benchmarks).

In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input.

| Model weights | With Base configuration and tokenizer | With NUPA configuration and tokenizer |
|---|---:|---:|
| NUPA, with no expert transfer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 17.07% BFCL-Parity |
| NUPA, with 16 BFCL experts per layer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 21.14% BFCL-Parity |

In another ablation, restoring NUPA’s own special-token rows increased NUPA200 from 29.00% to 39.00%. These rows represent control tokens, such as message boundaries.

COMMENT: Agent experimental design here was flawed and will require a follow-up study.

The agent drifted from adding specialist capabilities to the Base model almost immediately during the campaign and instead focused on combining the two specialists. We will conduct a follow-up study where we enforce that specialist changes may only target a small, measured fraction of the base model's weights, and perhaps try to control for the tokenizer confound as well.
```

</details>

With NUPA weights held fixed, changing the configuration and tokenizer moved BFCL-Parity from 0.81% to 17.07%, so model metadata is a material confound. [PR #9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) already adds aligned merging and historical artifacts, but its tools do not enforce the later rule that at least 75% of Base weights stay unchanged.

**Relevant code**
- [README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/README.md#L26-L28) — retention and replay limits.
- [select_experts.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/select_experts.py#L19-L56) — ranked and random expert recipes.

Use #9974 for the follow-up study after review; a second merger implementation would overlap it.

1. Pin the Base, NUPA, and BFCL checkpoint revisions. Keep Base's configuration, tokenizer, chat template, and generation settings fixed for every Base-anchored candidate. Verify tensor and expert-row alignment and specify how donor special-token rows are handled before merging.
2. Audit each export against Base at its stored dtype. Count unchanged scalar weights globally and by component, including embeddings, attention, routers, shared experts, and routed experts; reject candidates that change more than 25% of Base weights.
3. Collect fresh activation measurements, since the archive lacks raw transcripts for exact replay. Compare Base-anchored sequential NUPA/BFCL transfers at predeclared 5%, 10%, and 25% change budgets against matched random expert transfers. Include Base, each specialist, and the prior unconstrained best as reference checkpoints.
4. Evaluate NUPA200, BFCL-Parity, and the complete policy cohort with identical prompts and decoding. Set acceptable non-target regressions before scoring, inspect output-format failures, and publish checkpoint revisions, recipes, changed-weight counts, scores, and negative results. Advance a merge only if it improves both targets within the weight budget and the preregistered retention limits.

spillover_issues.title: [Post-training][Model merging] Initial Experiments in Model Merging with Snowball 67B A2B

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
TL;DR: Model merging is a promising direction for Marin: different Grug/Snowball checkpoints have complementary strengths, but we do not yet have a reliable way to combine them while preserving the base model's other capabilities. Cheap weight-space operations could make this orders of magnitude less expensive than on-policy distillation (OPD). We would benefit from expert input on how to make that tradeoff work for our mixture-of-experts (MoE) models.

The policy evaluation tracker illustrates the problem (percentages; higher is better):

| Checkpoint | MATH500 | GPQA-Diamond | HumanEval+ | NUPA | BFCL-Parity/Pi |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [Grug Antidoom Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02) | 95.00 | 67.30 | 72.60 | 0.10 | 5.70 |
| [Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92) | 89.60 | 42.90 | 68.90 | 40.60 | 16.30 |
| [Grug Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04) | 92.60 | 63.00 | 86.60 | 0.30 | 43.90 |

Source: [policy-tracker snapshot](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/inputs/TRACKER.md). These are policy NUPA scores; the merge study instead optimized NUPA200, a 200-task subset of the policy’s 5,000-task panel. BFCL-Parity/Pi is the policy's tool-use evaluation with the Pi agent. No checkpoint in this comparison achieves the best score in every column.

Our [initial study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975) shows both the appeal and the unresolved problem. Static merge construction typically required roughly 1e11–1e12 estimated arithmetic FLOPs per checkpoint, often without GPUs. This supports the prospect of a large compute advantage over OPD, which requires rollout generation and training; we have not run a matched OPD cost comparison. Evaluation and any calibration or expert-selection work add costs beyond static construction.

The best merge scored 36.50% on NUPA200 and 48.78% on BFCL-Parity, versus historical specialist references of 38.00% and 43.90%, respectively. But its recipe copied only 0.76% of all parameter values unchanged from the intended Base (Step12). On non-target benchmarks, it scored 89.80% MATH500 and 52.19% GPQA-Diamond, versus Base’s historical policy scores of 95.00% and 67.30%; these were not matched reruns. That study did not establish capability-preserving transfer into Base.

We would welcome advice from people with model-merging experience, especially on transferring specialist behavior into an existing MoE checkpoint with limited weight changes, handling expert/router compatibility and the tokenizer differences observed in #9975, and choosing retention evaluations that expose damage outside the target benchmarks.

Done when: expert feedback informs a concrete follow-up design with a fixed Base, explicit limits on weight changes, and pre-agreed target and non-target evaluation criteria.

spillover_issues.author: hammer
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Add native Grug / GrugMoE support to **upstream** `vllm-project/vllm` and `huggingface/transformers` so a published HF checkpoint (e.g. Snowball, #7366) loads and runs with stock libraries — no Marin fork required.

Today Grug is only runnable via Levanter/JAX or the Marin vLLM fork (https://github.com/marin-community/vllm); upstream vLLM and `transformers` do not know the architecture, so external users of a published checkpoint cannot `AutoModel.from_pretrained(...)` or `vllm serve` it. This is the external-usability gap noted in #6811 and carried into the publish task #7366.

This is intentionally gated: @yonromai flagged in #6811 that we should not pay the upstreaming overhead "until the Grug architecture is more stable." File this to track the work and revisit once the arch settles.

Prior/related work (all fork-scoped, not upstream):
- #6041 GrugMoE in Marin vLLM fork, TPU (closed) · #6042 same, GPU (closed)
- #6106 GrugMoE vLLM TPU support experiment (open)
- #7097 consolidate Marin's vLLM forks to one patch set (open)

### Definition of Done

- A `modeling_grug` implementation (ideally via `modular_transformers`) merged into upstream `huggingface/transformers`; a Grug config loads through `AutoConfig`/`AutoModel`.
- Grug/GrugMoE architecture supported in upstream `vllm-project/vllm` for inference.
- A published Snowball checkpoint (#7366) loads and generates with stock `transformers` + `vllm` (no Marin fork), with output parity vs the Levanter/JAX reference and the Marin vLLM fork.

Blocks external use in #7366.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Scope: not a code-change PR.** This is a tracking issue for cross-repo upstreaming into `huggingface/transformers` and `vllm-project/vllm`, explicitly gated (@yonromai in #6811: don't pay the upstreaming cost "until the Grug architecture is more stable"). No change lands in this repo, so this is analysis for a human to schedule rather than a PR.

# Research

Grug/GrugMoE has no upstream support: `transformers`/`vllm` don't know `model_type="grug_moe"`, so a published checkpoint only runs via Levanter/JAX or the Marin vLLM fork. The reference implementation is the pinned Snowball recipe; the HF-side surface (config class, AutoConfig registration, state-dict converters) already exists in-repo and is the natural source of truth to port.

**Relevant code**
- [`snowball.py#L74-L114`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L74-L114) — `GRUG_MOE_MODEL_TYPE`, `GrugMoeHfConfig`
- [`snowball.py#L880`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L880) — `AutoConfig.register(grug_moe, ...)`
- [`snowball.py#L721-L864`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L721-L864) — Levanter↔HF state-dict converters (canonical weight naming)
- [`grug_moe.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/grug_moe.py) — MoE routing/dispatch reference
- [`vllm_server.py#L74-L90`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_server.py#L74-L90) — `MARIN_FORK` exists precisely because upstream vLLM can't load `grug_moe`

# Proposed approach (for a human to schedule)

Two independent upstream tracks; both are external repos, neither is a marin PR.

1. **`huggingface/transformers`** — add `models/grug_moe/{configuration,modeling}_grug_moe.py`, ideally via `modular_transformers`. Port from `snowball.py`: `GrugMoeHfConfig` fields, and the architecture-specific pieces (QB-routed MoE with sigmoid combine + shared expert, GatedNorm, exclusive self-attention, dual short/long RoPE schedule). Weight naming must match [`snowball_to_state_dict`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L721-L864) so existing exports load unchanged. Register in `AutoConfig`/`AutoModelForCausalLM`.
2. **`vllm-project/vllm`** — add `model_executor/models/grug_moe.py` mirroring the HF module under vLLM's KV-cache + worker-sharding semantics; register it. This is what today's `marin-community/vllm` fork carries; upstreaming it feeds #7097 (one-fork consolidation).

**Parity gate (Definition of Done):** stock `transformers` + `vllm` load a published Snowball checkpoint (#7366) and match the Levanter/JAX reference and the Marin fork. In-repo E2E harness to reuse for validation: [`tests/vllm/test_grugmoe_real_checkpoint_e2e.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/vllm/test_grugmoe_real_checkpoint_e2e.py).

**Recommendation:** keep gated per #6811 until the arch settles; land HF first (unblocks `AutoModel` for #7366), then vLLM. No marin-side change is required until a follow-up flips `MARIN_FORK`→`UPSTREAM` once both land.

spillover_issues.author: hammer
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Publish the "Snowball" checkpoint — the Grug 67B-A2B intermediate cooldown trained on 2T tokens (of 10T) in #6811 — to Hugging Face so external users can try it. The hero run has landed and SFT/midtraining, chat templating, vLLM serving, and evals are green (announced 2026-07-17). Publishing was agreed in the #6811 thread: @hammer asked, @ClassicLarry and @yonromai concurred, with prerequisites noted below.

Final permanent checkpoint (Levanter/Grug format):
`gs://marin-us-central2/grug/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step39k-79ebf3/checkpoints/step-42150/`
(567 objects, ~539 GB; note step-**42150**, not 42149 — see https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6811#issuecomment-4952891213 correction by @yonromai). Regional mirrors already exist in `s3://marin-us-east-02a/...` and `gs://marin-us-east5/...`.

Prerequisites raised in the thread, which this task must resolve first:
- **Standardize the config against HF conventions** before export (@ClassicLarry).
- **Serialization contract for external use.** A Grug→safetensors export exists in `main` but was written for internal vLLM serving; it needs hardening for external consumers (@yonromai).
- **Inference-path caveat.** Grug is only runnable today via Levanter/JAX or the Marin vLLM fork (https://github.com/marin-community/vllm); upstream vLLM/transformers does not support the architecture. The HF model card must document this so external users know how to load it.

### Definition of Done

- Grug step-42150 checkpoint exported to safetensors with an HF-standard config, uploaded to a `marin-community` HF repo.
- Model card documents architecture (67B total / ~2B active MoE, d2560, 2T-token cooldown), provenance (links #6811), license, and the supported inference paths (Marin vLLM fork / Levanter), with a working load-and-generate snippet.
- Exported weights verified to produce outputs matching the source checkpoint under the Marin vLLM fork.

Parent hero run: #6811.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Actionability check — issue is actionable (clear DoD) but large (release + export infra, ~539 GB, HF upload, model card, parity verification). Per fix-issue scoping this warrants analysis, **not** a PR.
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight — no open PRs/issues for grug safetensors export or Snowball publish.
- [x] Locate existing export machinery and config mapping.
- [ ] Human review of the approach below before implementation.

# Research

A working Grug→safetensors export already exists, but it lives **inside the vLLM E2E test harness**, is wired to a fixed region, and uses an internal-serving weight layout — exactly the three prerequisites the #6811 thread flagged (HF-standard config, external serialization contract, documented inference path).

- The export itself is one `converter.save_pretrained(...)` call, sharded into 256 MB safetensors, buried in a test backend: [`grugmoe_real_checkpoint_backend.py#L362-L427`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/vllm/grugmoe_real_checkpoint_backend.py#L362-L427).
- It exports via a **legacy split-expert** state-dict layout, not the canonical `grugmoe_inference_state_dict`: [`#L266`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/vllm/grugmoe_real_checkpoint_backend.py#L266) vs [`model.py#L862`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L862) — this is the "which layout do external consumers get" contract to pin down.
- `to_hf_config()` emits **dual grug+HF field names** (`hidden_dim`+`hidden_size`, `num_experts`+`num_local_experts`, …) plus a private `grug_moe_artifact_schema_version` — this is the non-standard config @ClassicLarry wants normalized: [`model.py#L228-L265`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L228-L265).
- Region lock: the harness hard-requires `europe-west4` for every path ([`#L129`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/vllm/grugmoe_real_checkpoint_backend.py#L129)); the checkpoint is in `us-central2` (mirrors `us-east5` / `s3://marin-us-east-02a`). Reading 539 GB cross-region violates the AGENTS.md cost rule — export must run co-located with a mirror.
- HF push is already supported by the converter: `save_pretrained(..., upload_to_hf=RepoRef)` creates the repo and uploads: [`hf_checkpoints.py#L1027-L1137`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py#L1027-L1137). No model-card generation exists — the README must be authored and uploaded separately.

# Proposed Approach (for review — not yet implemented)

Extract the export from the test harness into a reusable, region-parameterized CLI (e.g. `experiments/grug/moe/export_to_hf.py`) and run it as a one-off release job co-located with a checkpoint mirror:

1. **Pin the serialization contract.** Decide canonical layout: reuse `grugmoe_inference_state_dict` (matches the Marin vLLM fork loader) vs the legacy split-expert layout the harness currently ships. Document tensor naming so the fork + Levanter both round-trip. This is the core "harden for external use" work.
2. **Standardize `config.json`.** Choose HF-canonical keys as authoritative (`hidden_size`, `num_local_experts`, `num_experts_per_tok`, `rms_norm_eps`, `num_hidden_layers`, …); keep the grug aliases only if the fork loader still reads them, otherwise drop them. Keep `architectures: ["GrugMoeForCausalLM"]` and the schema-version key.
3. **Region.** Run the export on a worker in `us-east5` (or `us-central2`) reading the local mirror; write the safetensors output to the same region, then upload to HF. No cross-region 539 GB reads.
4. **Upload** to `marin-community/<name>` via `save_pretrained(upload_to_hf=...)`, `private=True` first.
5. **Model card.** Author `README.md`: architecture (67B total / ~2B active MoE, d2560, 2T-of-10T cooldown, step-**42150**), provenance (link #6811), license, supported inference paths (Marin vLLM fork / Levanter — upstream vLLM/transformers unsupported), and a working load-and-generate snippet. Upload alongside weights.
6. **Verify parity.** Reuse the existing E2E vLLM parity check ([`test_grugmoe_real_checkpoint_e2e.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/vllm/test_grugmoe_real_checkpoint_e2e.py)) against the exported repo under the Marin fork to satisfy the DoD's "outputs match source checkpoint".

**Open questions for a human before I proceed:**
- Target HF repo name under `marin-community`, and license to declare.
- Canonical weight layout: `grugmoe_inference_state_dict` or the legacy split-expert layout the fork currently expects?
- Which region/machine to run the ~539 GB export on (TPU vs CPU worker; co-located mirror).
- Keep or drop the dual grug/HF config aliases (depends on the fork loader).

Given the scope (checkpoint-export infra + a large one-off release job, not a code bugfix), I'm stopping here for review rather than opening a PR.

spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This follow-up to PR #6841 tests the best review-ranked ways to make source-push expert-parallel MoE competitive on EP8 H100s. The useful path is the staged semantic implementation: round 1 kept the bf16 `dy` cast, adopted XLA gather-sum combine, and confirmed host-side planning is the largest structural blocker, while owner-sharded `dx` return and fused W13 zero-fill fixes were falsified. The apparent W2-return regression was later traced to the deliberate W2-from-H boundary switch, not branch drift; SPF-008 recovered part of that cost by moving route scaling to the output side (w2_return 7.08 -> 6.36 ms), but naive double-buffering hurt occupancy. Current recommendation: continue on staged semantic/device-sided planning and occupancy-neutral W2-from-H overlap; keep the fused persistent-kernel path quarantined until it passes an integrated numerical gate.

### Helpful links
- PR #6841: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6841
- Round-1 results: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7276#issuecomment-4997344962
- SPF-007 root-cause note: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7276#issuecomment-4999175606
- SPF-008 result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7276#issuecomment-5005358579
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Builds on #6597 / #6848 / PR #6841 at head `26711f86e`, target shape EP8 H100, 32768 tok/rank, top-k 4, 32 experts/rank, d2560/f1280, goal 250 useful TFLOP/s/rank fwd+bwd. Branch: `research/mcwitt/6841-source-push-followup`.

Ranked avenues (gain / effort):

1. `SPF-001` bf16-cast `dy` before the replicated reshard (`source_push_semantic_mlp.py:586`): all-gather payload 2.35 -> 1.17 GB, est. ~5.8 ms off the 63.0 ms API. S.
2. `SPF-002` switch dx return to the existing owner-sharded `psum_scatter` wrapper (`source_push_semantic_mlp.py:621`): all-reduce 4.70 -> 2.35 GB/rank, est. 3-6 ms. S.
3. `SPF-003a` measure unlogged tip commit `26711f86e` (grouped W13 raw gathers) vs the 23.025 ms fused-W13 baseline. Free.
4. `SPF-003b` fused W13-bwd unconditionally remote-writes a zero tile then overwrites it (`source_push_semantic_fused_w13_backward.py:1040`): 2x NVLink bytes on dX return, est. 2-4 ms of 135.5. S.
5. `SPF-004` combine kernel runs at ~21% of HBM roofline (per-row scalar loads, `source_push_combine.py:145`): 1.34 -> ~0.5 ms. S.
6. `SPF-005` host-side numpy planner cost at target shape is excluded from every benchmark number (O(268M) element ops/plan, `source_push_plan.py:636`): measure it. S, CPU-only.
7. Source-push dy route (fix dcombine in_specs `source_push_semantic_backward_pallas.py:2280`, reuse existing dy-route remote-write kernel + global phase barrier): rest of the 11.6 ms API tax. M-L.
8. W2-return kernel double-buffering + deferred `wait_smem_to_gmem` (`source_push_w2_return.py:680-765`): 4.05 -> ~2.7 ms. M.
9. Correctness cluster: single-jit remote-write completion barrier is scalar-only (`source_push_forward.py:1109`); fused dX-return has no wait on `ready_sem` before the combine kernel; integrated numerical gate FUSED-MOE-094 failed (y max-abs-diff 1024) and was never re-cleared. S-M, blocking for fused promotion.
10. SM-carveout restructure (persistent SM-capped comm kernels + pipelined near-stock GEMM consumers; de-fuse W2-return/combine as a dense fixed-shape permute): only credible route to 250. L, design first.

## Hypothesis or Goal

The S-effort tier (1+2+5) takes the honest API from 63.0 to ~50-52 ms (~150 useful) with grad parity, converging on the 44.2 ms manual bound; measurements 3/6 decide where the next M/L unit of work goes.

## Status

Round 1 complete (2026-07-16): SPF-001 keep (-1.87 ms, API 61.008 ms / 126.79 useful), SPF-002 falsified (VJP sharding contract), SPF-003a real but modest (-1.11%), SPF-003b falsified, SPF-004 adopt (XLA combine, bitwise-identical, 1745 GB/s) + W2 hoist keep, SPF-005 confirmed ~190x (380 ms/plan; ~1.85 s public path). New open items: SPF-006 compare-gate regression bisect. SPF-007 resolved from records (no bisect needed): the w2_return 4.05->7.08 ms jump is the deliberate W2-from-H boundary switch (`ae1c9aed1`+`e8fbfa85e`, 2026-07-03), measured contemporaneously; reclassified as avenue-8 kernel work. See round-1 comment and SPF-007 comment. SPF-008 (2026-07-17): avenue 8 executed on branch `spf/008-w2-from-h-kernel` — output-side route scaling ADOPTED (w2_return 7.077 -> 6.355 ms, total 16.72 -> 15.97; numerics bit-match the pre-change smoke; no new pytest failures vs head), 2-stage double-buffering FALSIFIED (8.57 ms: 2x SMEM halves CTA occupancy) and reverted; ~1.4 ms to the ~5.0 ms from_h floor remains, needs an occupancy-neutral overlap design. See SPF-008 comment. 2026-07-17: thread refocused on B200 (production priority) — continues in #7333 (SPB series); this issue is the H100 phase (retitled). Remaining H100 items (SPF-006 compare-gate bisect, occupancy-neutral W2-from-H overlap) deprioritized pending the SPB-001 gate.

## Links

* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/6841-source-push-followup.md` on `research/mcwitt/6841-source-push-followup`
* Prior logbooks: `.agents/logbooks/6597-moe-mgpu-forward.md`, `.agents/logbooks/6597-moe-fused-comm-tensorcore.md`
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

* 2026-07-17: refocus on B200 — production priority; B200 phase opened as #7333 (SPB series); this issue scoped to H100.
* 2026-07-16: perf spend goes to the staged semantic path; fused path gets free measurements + S-effort fixes only until it passes a finite integrated numerical gate.
* 2026-07-16: adopt XLA gather-sum combine (bitwise-identical, faster, deletes a kernel); keep bf16-dy cast and W2 weight-copy hoist; discard zero-fill fix and owner-sharded dx return.
* 2026-07-16: production viability of the public source-push API is gated on device-siding the planner (SPF-005) before any further kernel tuning; next perf unit of work is the SPF-007 bisect.
* 2026-07-17: SPF-008 — adopt output-side route scaling on the W2-from-H kernels (branch `spf/008-w2-from-h-kernel`, `aa38972c8`; -0.72 ms w2_return); reject naive double-buffering for these Lane kernels — overlap designs must keep SMEM under ~112 KB/CTA to preserve 2 CTAs/SM.
* 2026-07-16: SPF-007 closed without a bisect — root cause identified from the 6597 logbook records (W2-from-H switch is a priced-in H-boundary cost, head is +0.03 ms over the day-one 7.048 ms measurement); the recovery path is avenue 8 (output-side route scaling + double-buffered k-loop, ~4.5-5 ms target vs 6.80 ms post-hoist).

## Conclusion

🤖 SPF round 1 complete — all five experiments ran; results below (logbook has exact commands/jobs; branch `research/mcwitt/6841-source-push-followup` + `spf/00*` experiment branches).

| ID | Result | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| SPF-001 bf16 dy before the replicated reshard | API fwd+bwd 62.876 -> **61.008 ms** (126.79 useful), grad parity within accepted threshold | Keep (below the pre-registered 4 ms bar — the fp32 dy AG only costs ~3.7 ms at head — but zero-risk and the best-performing arm). `spf/001-backward-quick-wins` @ `2fc968f52` |

| SPF-003b fused W13-bwd zero-fill double-write fix | Bit-exact, but +0.32 ms vs control | **Falsified** — duplicate NVLink zero-writes were fully overlapped; reverted |
| SPF-004 combine via plain XLA gather-sum | **0.481 ms / 1745 GB/s**, bitwise-identical to the Pallas kernel, deterministic | **Adopt** (`spf/004-combine-roofline` @ `2ece2c284`); also W2 from_h weight-copy hoist kept (-3.9% stage) |

New issues found while measuring:
- **SPF-006**: reduced-shape fused-W13 compare `valid_error_count` regressed 0 -> 5 -> 3 somewhere in `d2ce47ca35..088831b4b` (72 commits); blocks promotion from that segment until bisected.

- Iris: `/tmp/iris` port-lock dir owned by another OS user breaks auto-tunnel for everyone else (`iris/cluster/backends/types.py:70-97` swallows PermissionError per port); and the current `cuda_toolchain_setup_script` `--offline` cudnn reinstall fails on cold-cache nodes.

State of the ladder: honest API 63.0 -> 61.0 ms (SPF-001); combine and W2-hoist wins live on the forward path; `ring` (38.2 ms / 202 useful) still leads. Next highest-leverage: bisect SPF-007, then avenue 7 (source-push dy; requires the owner-sharded-x boundary change SPF-002 exposed) and the avenue-10 SM-carveout design.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **SPF-007 resolved — no bisect needed.** The w2_return 4.05 → 7.08 ms "regression" is a single step change with a contemporaneous paper trail, not branch drift:

- 4.050 ms logged at `89f3267fc` (2026-07-03 13:12) with the post-SwiGLU `_sharded_w2_return_direct_to_source_kernel`.
- `ae1c9aed1` "Wire source-push forward through H" + `e8fbfa85e` "Fix source-push W2-from-H lowering" (17:39/17:59 the same day) switched the staged forward to `_sharded_w2_from_h_return_direct_to_source_kernel` so the MLP-level custom VJP gets its H-checkpoint residual.
- 7.048 ms was measured at 18:04 that evening and attributed to the W2-from-H prologue (`6597-moe-mgpu-forward.md:4623`); head measures 7.077 ms — the other ~250 commits in the range contributed ~nothing.

Mechanism (from the kernel diff): ~2.5× M-side GMEM traffic (gate+up = 2I vs I, plus a k-invariant route-weight tile reloaded every k iteration until the SPF-004 hoist), a serial fp32 SwiGLU through an extra SMEM round-trip between TMA and WGMMA, and a single-buffered k-loop with `wgmma_wait(0)` inside — no overlap of loads/elementwise/wgmma.

Reclassified from "regression bisect" to **avenue 8 kernel work**, with a sharpened plan: (1) move route scaling to the output tile — exact algebra, `(diag(w)·A)·W2 = diag(w)·(A·W2)` — deleting `weight_smem` from the loop; (2) double-buffer + deferred `wgmma_wait` so SwiGLU overlaps the next tile's TMA. Direct-kernel parity is not expected (2× hidden bytes is inherent to the H boundary), but roofline says only ~1 ms of the +3 ms is bytes; ~4.5–5 ms vs 6.80 ms post-hoist looks reachable.

Logbook: SPF-007 entry on `research/mcwitt/6841-source-push-followup` (`2926b0f78`).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **SPF-008 — avenue-8 executed: output-side route scaling adopted (w2_return 7.08 → 6.36 ms); double-buffering falsified by occupancy**

Branch `spf/008-w2-from-h-kernel` (off PR head `26711f86e`, tip `882f2d3d5`).

**Adopted (`aa38972c8`).** The route weight is per-row, so `(diag(w)·A)·W2 = diag(w)·(A·W2)`: the from_h/from_compact_h kernels now scale the fp32 accumulator once after the k-loop instead of multiplying the weight into every activation tile. This deletes the k-invariant weight-tile reload (subsumes the SPF-004 hoist), the host-side `[rows, block_k]` route-weight expansion, and one multiply per element in the serial SwiGLU. The 2026-07-03 "cannot load the block_m=64 route-weight vector" lowering blocker does not apply post-GEMM — `mgpu.load(..., Layout.WGMMA.reduce(1))` + broadcast into the accumulator lowers fine.

Measured (`/marin/spf008-mid-aa38972c8`, 216 profile, staged_host_sync, roughly_balanced cf1.25, 5 repeats): **w2_return 6.355 ms** (head 7.077, hoist 6.803), **total 15.970 ms** (head 16.724), w13 8.576, combine 0.898. Numerics: reduced-shape `--check` max_abs_diff `0.00048828125`, bit-identical to the pre-change 2026-07-03 smoke. H100 `-k source_push` pytest: same `2 failed, 13 passed` as unmodified head (both failures pre-existing, confirmed by control job `/marin/spf008-headctl-pytest-26711f86e`).

**Falsified (`2c0f60a70`, reverted).** The planned 2-stage double-buffered k-loop with deferred `wgmma_wait(1)` made it **worse**: 8.573 ms (`/marin/spf008-tipbench-2c0f60a70`). Doubling pipeline SMEM 80→160 KB/CTA halves co-resident CTAs per SM from 2 to 1, and the inter-CTA interleaving that was hiding the serial TMA→SwiGLU→wgmma chain is worth more than the intra-CTA pipeline. Lesson: overlap schemes for these Lane kernels must stay under ~112 KB/CTA (2 CTAs/SM) — in-place activation staging or warp specialization, not naive full double-buffering.

**Where this leaves avenue 8**: from_h floor is ~5.0 ms (direct 4.05 + ~1 ms inherent H-boundary bytes); 6.36 achieved; ~1.4 ms of serialization overhead remains for an occupancy-neutral design. Logbook entry: SPF-008 on `research/mcwitt/6841-source-push-followup`.

spillover_issues.author: yonromai
spillover_issues.body:
## Goal

Use a supported PyTorch CUDA 13 build alongside JAX CUDA 13, and keep only the direct version pins that protect a demonstrated compatibility boundary. The uv lock should provide reproducibility; package requirements should use ranges where safe.

## Current blocker

`marin-core[gpu]` currently resolves:

- JAX on CUDA 13 with `nvidia-cublas>=13.2.0.9`.
- PyTorch 2.11 from the cu128 index with separate CUDA 12 runtime packages.

The PyTorch cu130 wheel cannot replace cu128 as-is: it requires `cuda-toolkit[cublas]==13.0.2`, which pins `nvidia-cublas==13.1.0.3` and conflicts with Marin’s B200 cuBLAS floor.

## Work

1. Find a supported PyTorch CUDA 13 resolution that retains Marin’s H100 NCCL and B200 cuBLAS guards. Prefer a newer compatible release over overriding an upstream exact CUDA-library dependency.
2. Audit the direct GPU requirements for `torch`, `torchvision`, and the CUDA libraries:
   - Document why each exact pin or bounded range is necessary.
   - Replace exact application-level pins with compatible ranges where the lockfile and upstream dependency metadata are sufficient.
   - Keep hardware safety floors such as cuBLAS/NCCL until validation proves they are obsolete.
3. Update the PyTorch index selection and uv lock.
4. Validate imports, device execution, matmul, and collectives on H100 and B200; run the existing H100 GPU canary.

## Acceptance criteria

- `marin-core[gpu]` installs one coherent CUDA 13 environment without per-job overrides.
- PyTorch and TorchVision resolve as a compatible pair.
- The resolved cuBLAS and NCCL versions retain the existing B200 and H100 fixes.
- Every remaining direct exact pin has a nearby compatibility rationale; otherwise it is expressed as the narrowest validated range.
- H100 and B200 smoke tests pass, and the H100 GPU canary passes.

<details>
<summary>Why the current constraints exist</summary>

- **Torch 2.11:** selected in #5379 because Torch 2.10 cu128 pinned NCCL 2.27.5, which reproduced a CoreWeave H100 all-to-all failure. Torch 2.11 cu128 brought NCCL 2.28.9, which passed the probe.
- **TorchVision 0.26:** this is the native-extension compatibility pair for Torch 2.11. PR #6346 demonstrated why changing Torch without changing TorchVision is unsafe.
- **cuBLAS floor:** `nvidia-cublas>=13.2.0.9` was added in #5428 after older CUDA 13 builds warned on B200. Marin does not directly exact-pin cuBLAS; uv records the selected version in the lock.
- **cu128 index:** retained because the available Torch cu130 metadata exact-pinned cuBLAS below that B200 floor.
- **vLLM:** the selected vLLM revision also pins its build/runtime Torch and TorchVision pair exactly. Relaxing Marin alone may therefore not be enough for GPU vLLM; any required fork change belongs with #7135.

</details>

Blocks #7135. The downstream `marin-serve --gpu` integration remains tracked by #7111.

comments.author: weaverbot
comments.body:
🤖 Cross-ref from PR #7303 (merged).

#7303 completed `serve_and_eval`'s GPU vLLM path by overlaying Marin's forked CUDA vLLM onto the serve venv (`VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 … --torch-backend=cu130 "vllm @ git+<fork>@<rev>" runai-model-streamer[s3]`), then serving it with the default `WorkspaceVllm` launcher. Its note reads "drop the overlay for `marin-core[vllm-gpu]` once #7134 lands."

On #7303, @rjpower asked us to reconsider that target. Rather than wait on a managed `vllm-gpu` extra, the direction is to productionize the launcher path: extend the isolated CUDA vLLM launcher already merged in #7133 with a source selector (`VllmType {UPSTREAM, MARIN_FORK}`), so `marin.inference` serves both stock and fork vLLM through one `uvx` launcher — chosen by the model, not the accelerator. (Design + diagrams in the artifact; discussion mirrored on #7135.)

Directly relevant to this issue: the overlay runs `--torch-backend=cu130`, which is exactly what a managed `gpu` extra cannot carry today. The extra is pinned to the `pytorch-cu128` index because cu130's cuBLAS sits below Marin's B200 floor (`nvidia-cublas>=13.2.0.9`) — this issue's own stated blocker. An isolated `uvx` launcher runs cu130 in a throwaway env without dragging cuBLAS into the workspace resolution, so it can retire the #7303 overlay *without* first resolving the CUDA-13 unification.

Net: #7134 stays valuable for a single coherent managed GPU image, but it is no longer the blocker for the serve/eval path — that path can standardize on the launcher independently.

Full research, project-dependency diagrams, and the proposed design: https://loom.oa.dev/s/ms4p9i4w/artifacts/vllm-serve-productionization

This issue stays open on its own merits: the CUDA-13 managed-stack unification, the direct version-pin audit, and the B200/H100 canary are all untouched by that PR — the launcher runs cu130 in an isolated uvx env precisely to sidestep the cuBLAS/B200 floor that blocks the managed extra here.
