# Research

Iris is pure-IAP for external clusters: the controller mints **no** user token ([`main.py#L127-L132`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/main.py#L127-L132)). `iris login` runs the desktop-OAuth browser flow and caches only a long-lived **IAP edge refresh token** per cluster at `~/.config/marin/credentials/<cluster>.json` ([`credential_store.py#L39-L56`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/credential_store.py#L39-L56)). Email + expiry are **not stored** — they live in the short-lived OIDC ID token that `IapRefreshTokenProvider` re-mints from the refresh token on each request ([`auth.py#L200-L235`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/auth.py#L200-L235)). Non-IAP clusters need no login (loopback/CIDR trust). No `login status`/`whoami` command exists today; `GetCurrentUser` RPC returns only `user_id`+`role` ([`service.py#L2774-L2785`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/service.py#L2774-L2785)), not email/expiry, and needs a live connection.

**Relevant code**
- [`main.py#L118-L180`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/main.py#L118-L180) — `iris login`; `_id_token` from the flow is **discarded** (L162)
- [`credential_store.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/credential_store.py) — per-cluster store; `load_credentials`, `credentials_dir()`, free-form `metadata`
- [`credentials.py#L77-L128`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/credentials.py#L77-L128) — `iap_edge_provider`, login-method resolution
- [`connect.py#L259-L265`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/connect.py#L259-L265) — `iap_config()` → is this cluster IAP-fronted
- [`cluster.py#L271-L280`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L271-L280) — `iris cluster list` uses `list_cluster_configs(IRIS_CLUSTER_CONFIG_DIRS)`

# Proposed Design

New command **`iris whoami [--all] [--format text|json]`** (a new top-level command; `login` is a plain `@iris.command()`, not a group, so `iris login status` would require converting it — a larger UX change I'd avoid). Default = current cluster; `--all` = every configured cluster.

Per cluster, dump:

| field | source |
|---|---|
| cluster | `CredentialRecord.cluster` / config name |
| login method | `iap` if `iap_config(config)` else `none (network trust)`; `not logged in` if IAP but no cached record |
| email | `email` claim of the IAP ID token |
| token expiry | `exp` claim of the IAP ID token |
| endpoint | `CredentialRecord.endpoint` |

Enumerate via `list_cluster_configs(IRIS_CLUSTER_CONFIG_DIRS)` × cached files under `credentials_dir()`.

**Open decision — where email/expiry come from (needs your call):**
1. **Mint-on-demand** (recommended): call `IapRefreshTokenProvider.get_token()` then `google.auth.jwt.decode(token, verify=False)` for `email`/`exp`. Accurate, works for logins done before this change, but makes a network call and shows the *re-minted* ID token's ~1h expiry (the cached refresh token has no fixed expiry — it's valid until revoked). On `IapLoginRequired`/refresh failure → show `expired — run iris login`.
2. **Store-at-login**: decode the already-returned `_id_token` at login (`main.py#L162`), stash `email` in `record.metadata`. No network, but only populated for future logins and can't show live expiry.

I lean #1 (offline-graceful), optionally also doing #2 so email shows without a network round-trip. Estimated ~70–90 lines + one behavior test (fake a `CredentialRecord`, assert the dump renders method/email/expiry; assert the not-logged-in path).

Per the agent rubric this is a **new feature**, so I'm holding here for a human to confirm the command name and the email/expiry source (#1 vs #2 vs both) before implementing. Reply with a preference and I'll open the PR.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
We'd like Marin to be more cross-agent friendly: agents that are less aggressive at pulling from GH context are suffering on our repo currently due to a lack of easy documentation and search features.

Build on existing work from mumwelt and #7035 and try rolling out some interventions to improve cross-agent performance. The biggest lifts appear to be from:

* semantic search integration: give agents a replacement for e.g. `rg` or `grep` which can identify important code lines quickly
* "wiki" feature for sharing important workflows in repo

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Scope:** Design/rollout task spanning tooling + docs + agent skills, and it builds directly on the still-open PR #7035. Too large and too dependent on unmerged work for an agent PR — analysis and a staged proposal below for a human to sign off before implementation.

## Research

The measurement half of this ask already exists in #7035 (open PR `weaver/analyze-context-efficiency`, not yet on `main`). Its two experiments quantify exactly the two interventions this issue names, and one result reframes the ask:

- **Semantic search — strong win.** Over 150 queries mined from real agent sessions, a local dense index (fastembed `bge-small` + cosine) beats ripgrep: top-1 judge-hit **0.42 vs 0.19**, reaching a satisfying answer at **~1,882 vs ~5,865 snippet tokens** — locating code in ~1/3 the carried tokens. **BM25 captures ~half the ranking gain at ~1/600th the build cost** (no model download, no GPU, runs headless).
- **Wiki — reframe it.** A per-fact wiki nets only ~0.3% of budget because **556 of 569** proposed article topics never recur across sessions. What pays back is **per-subsystem architecture docs** — which Marin already partly has (`AGENTS.md`, `OPS.md`, `.agents/skills/`). Any persistent memory must be **retrieval-gated**: the always-on prelude is already 16.9% of the budget, re-read every turn, so a wiki that loads unconditionally makes things worse.

**Relevant code / prior art**
- #7035 — measurement pipeline + reports (dependency; land first)
- `experiments/code_search_eval/REPORT.md` (in #7035) — BM25 vs dense vs ripgrep numbers
- `experiments/context_efficiency/REPORT.md` (in #7035) — wiki 0.3%, prelude 16.9%
- `.agents/skills/` (37 skills) + `AGENTS.md` / `OPS.md` — existing cross-agent doc surface to extend, not duplicate
- No existing semantic/BM25 code-search tooling in the repo (`rg` for `fastembed|bm25|code.?index` outside `experiments/` is empty), so this is greenfield tooling.

## Proposed approach (for review)

Cross-agent friendliness is the real goal (issue: agents that pull less GH context suffer), so every intervention must be **discoverable from the repo alone** — a committed CLI + a skill, not a GH-hosted wiki.

1. **Dependency: merge #7035 first.** It carries the eval harness these choices rest on; rolling out before it lands means shipping unmeasured.
2. **Ship code search as a committed CLI + skill, BM25 first.** BM25 is the low-risk default: half the token savings, ~1/600th build cost, no model/GPU, works in headless/cron agents. Wrap the `code_search_eval` winner as a `scripts/` CLI + a `search-code` skill so any agent finds it without GH context. Add the dense `bge-small` index as an opt-in higher-recall mode behind the same interface (separate code paths, not a boolean flag).
3. **Do NOT build a per-fact wiki.** Instead formalize **per-subsystem architecture docs** (extend existing `AGENTS.md`/`OPS.md`) and add a lightweight discovery index so agents locate them. Keep all of it retrieval-gated — nothing new in the always-on prelude.
4. **Measure the rollout against #7035's harness** rather than asserting wins, so we can tell whether BM25-default is enough before paying for the dense index in CI.

Each of steps 2-4 is its own PR-sized chunk (>100 LOC, new tooling + skill + docs). Happy to take the first concrete slice — most likely **step 2, the BM25 CLI + `search-code` skill** — as a standalone PR once #7035 lands and a human confirms this staging. The sequencing and the wiki reframe are the two decisions worth a human call before I write code.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
Part of #7045 (infra — SFT with confidence).

**Request:** add a training-only DenseMixer-style dense-forward + straight-through router gradient for Levanter's MoE models (Qwen3-MoE, Mixtral), gated behind a config flag, targeted at MoE **SFT / small-scale midtraining / extended pretraining**. Reference implementation: [`yaof20/DenseMixer`](https://github.com/yaof20/DenseMixer) ("Improving MoE Post-Training with Precise Router Gradients"), integrated in Axolotl as `integrations/densemixer/`.

### What's missing today

Levanter's MoE forward is the conventional sparse one: `src/levanter/models/qwen3_moe.py:324-325` does `softmax` then `jax.lax.top_k` and dispatches **only the selected experts** (`router_aux_loss_coef = 0.001`, `qwen3_moe.py:71`). No dense-forward / STE / counterfactual-router path exists in `src/levanter` (grep-negative).

Because the forward only ever computes the selected experts, the autograd graph contains **no node for the non-selected experts' logits** → the task-loss gradient to a non-selected expert's router logit is **exactly zero**. The only signal those logits get is the aux load-balancing loss, which targets utilization uniformity, not task-optimal routing. So the router cannot learn the counterfactual "expert *j* would have been better for this token." This is a property of the forward graph, so it is equally true in pretraining and SFT.

### Why it matters *particularly* for SFT / midtraining (the motivation)

At post-training the experts are **already specialized**, and under SFT their contents barely move — low LR (~1e-5 vs pretrain ~2e-4), few epochs, and in LoRA the expert FFNs are frozen outright. So the dominant *available* lever is **re-routing tokens among the existing experts**, not rewriting the experts themselves — and re-routing is exactly the gradient that the sparse forward withholds. The expected advantage from getting routing right is therefore highest precisely in this regime.

The four things that let pretraining amortize the weak router gradient all invert in post-training:

1. **Distribution shift → the router must *re-route*, not just route.** SFT data (instruction/reasoning/tool-use/chat) has a different optimal expert assignment than web text; picking the better of two sharply-different specialists is the counterfactual signal the sparse forward drops.
2. **Experts are specialized, so mis-routing is costly** — and the counterfactual signal is most valuable exactly when specialization is highest.
3. **Few steps / low LR / small data can't drown a weak per-step gradient** the way trillions of pretraining tokens could.
4. **The aux loss is attenuated** in SFT (it fights the SFT signal), weakening the one channel that touched non-selected logits.

Net: conventional SFT still gives gradient to the *selected* experts' logits (through the top-k softmax), so it can **intensify** the pretrained routing but **cannot redirect** it. That is the precise sense in which the router is "effectively frozen" during conventional MoE FT — and it lines up with DenseMixer's own ablations showing **frozen-router FT ≈ conventional FT** (their Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B table: frozen 44.56 vs conventional 43.76 avg), i.e. the conventional router gradient is too weak to move the policy off its pretrained attractor. (Numbers are DenseMixer's, not independently reproduced here.)

**Worst case (sharpest benefit): LoRA or low-LR full-FT on a specialized MoE with real distribution shift.** The experts are (nearly) frozen, so the router is the *only* routing-adaptive knob — and it is the one component whose gradient is broken.

### The mechanism (training-only, zero inference change)

DenseMixer patches only the training forward of the sparse MoE block:

1. **Full softmax over all experts + compute every expert for every token**, building `dense_outputs = Σ_all E_i(x)·w_i` alongside the conventional `sparse_outputs = Σ_topk E_i(x)·w_i`.
2. **STE combine:** `final = sparse_outputs.detach() + (dense_outputs - dense_outputs.detach())`. Forward value = the sparse output (numerically identical to stock MoE, same loss); backward gradient = the *dense* gradient, which flows through all experts' outputs and the full softmax → non-selected router logits now get task-loss gradient ∝ `E_i(x)·w_i`.
3. **Per-expert gradient hook** zeros the gradient into each expert's *params* for tokens that didn't select it, so expert-weight updates stay sparse. Net: **router gets the dense all-experts gradient; experts get the conventional sparse param gradient.**

Serving is untouched — the patched path runs only in training, so the exported/served model is bit-for-bit the stock sparse forward.

### Cost caveat (so this is a real cost/benefit call, not a free win)

The dense training forward computes ~N/k× the expert-FFN FLOPs per step (e.g. 128 experts / top-8 ≈ 16× for Qwen3-235B-A22B). That is a training-only cost; DenseMixer ships an `efficiency_analysis/` folder for exactly this reason. The gain magnitude tracks how much routing adaptation the SFT actually needs — it widens with distribution-shift magnitude, expert specialization, and LoRA-vs-full-FT; it is small when SFT data is near-distribution and you full-FT at a non-trivial LR. A config flag (default off) keeps it opt-in for the regimes where re-routing is the main lever.

cc @rjpower

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment explored whether free generation from strong base models can reveal pretraining coverage gaps that ordinary evals miss. The infrastructure direction made progress: a TPU-native sampler and latent-topic discovery path were prototyped, and smoke runs wrote reusable artifacts. The main scientific result so far is negative for tokenizer-vocab bigrams: both `r1` and `r2` completed, but Qwen collapsed bare two-word prompts into generic explanatory continuations, with 43/48 prompts sharing the same first token in at least 75% of samples and no useful improvement from expanding from the original prompt. Do not keep tuning the content-word bigram path; if this line continues, use a weaker launch family or a scorer that discounts generic preambles and validates candidates with the pairwise BPB gap workflow.

### Helpful links
- Initial sampler implementation note: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5006#issuecomment-4307017787
- First latent-topic smoke: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5006#issuecomment-4316637640
- Bigram `r1` result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5006#issuecomment-4316819223
- Bigram dead-end decision: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5006#issuecomment-4317162165
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description
Use free generation from strong base models as an eval-discovery tool for pretraining blind spots. Start with Qwen3, then compare against Llama, Gemma, and other strong bases where available. The goal is to find surface-form families that strong models naturally continue but Marin may not cover well in Paloma, uncheatable evals, raw technical text, or capability eval slices.

This is hypothesis generation, not evidence by itself. Any sampled category should be checked against real held-out documents and then validated with pairwise gap/PPL before changing data mixtures.

## Hypothesis or Goal
Sampling with both empty prompts and seeded prefixes will surface missing or under-covered distributions such as raw URLs, package metadata, tables, logs, schemas, notebooks, compiler output, non-English technical docs, citations, mixed prose-code formats, and unusual whitespace/layout patterns. Agent-assisted clustering can turn samples into candidate eval slices, but each cluster needs a real source and a coverage decision: already covered, add eval only, add data work, or ignore.

### Links
* Parent confidence epic: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5005
* Gap finder: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4934
* Raw technical text: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4961
* Capability evals: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4963

## Results

**Research**

Out of scope for a single small PR — this is a multi-stage research workflow (free generation → clustering → surface-form labels → validation via pairwise BPB). Gating dependency: the byte-aligned perplexity-gap report referenced in the linked runs has not landed on `main` yet; it lives on `codex/perplexity-gap-finder` at `890b8b2e7` and is tracked by #4934. Sampling work can start now, but validation hooks need #4934 to merge first (or to land as part of this effort).

Duplicate-work check: no overlapping open PR or issue. #4961 is the downstream data-work consumer; #4963 is the downstream eval-register consumer. This issue owns only the hypothesis-generation pipeline that feeds both.

**Relevant code**
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_server.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_server.py) — native/Docker vLLM sidecar, TPU+GPU
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx) — async_vllm / vllm / levanter sampling backends
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/uncheatable_eval.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/uncheatable_eval.py) — raw held-out docs template (Wikipedia, GH, arXiv, BBC)
- [`experiments/evals/exp1600_uncheatable_evals.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/exp1600_uncheatable_evals.py) — raw-doc PPL eval flow (wiring template)
- `codex/perplexity-gap-finder@890b8b2e7` — byte-aligned BPB gap report (blocked on #4934 landing)

Gaps on `main`: no free-generation harness, no embedding/clustering pipeline, no surface-form categorizer, and no gap report to validate against until #4934 lands.

**Proposed Approach**

Land this as three independently reviewable PRs rather than one blob.

PR 1 — `strong_model_sampler` (~300 LOC). New module at `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/coverage_sampler.py`. Thin wrapper over the existing vLLM backend in `inference_ctx/vllm.py` that drives a configured strong base (Qwen3-8B first, then Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B) over two prompt regimes: (a) empty / BOS-only, (b) short seeded prefixes drawn from Paloma + Uncheatable domain samples. Output: sharded JSONL of `{model, prompt_regime, seed_source, sample_text, logprobs_summary}` on GCS. Config is a dataclass (no env-var dispatch); reuses `VllmServerHandle` — do not fork a parallel inference path.

PR 2 — `sample_clustering` (~400 LOC). New module at `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/coverage_clustering.py`. Embed samples with a small off-the-shelf encoder (bge-small or e5-small via HF), cluster with HDBSCAN, then have an agent label each cluster with a surface-form tag (URLs, package metadata, tables, logs, schemas, notebooks, compiler output, non-English technical docs, citations, mixed prose-code, unusual whitespace). Output: parquet of `{cluster_id, label, examples, size, source_models}` plus an HTML report. No new provider SDK — reuse `anthropic` or the existing eval-LLM plumbing for labeling.

PR 3 — `coverage_gap_validation` (~200 LOC, gated on #4934). For each labeled cluster, pull matched real documents from Paloma + Uncheatable + `datakit/download/*` and run the byte-aligned BPB gap report from #4934. Emit a per-cluster verdict: `already_covered` / `add_eval_only` / `add_data_work` / `ignore`. Wire into `experiments/evals/` as `exp_coverage_gap_discovery.py` mirroring `exp_model_perplexity_gap_marin_vs_llama.py`.

Scope caveats worth sign-off before coding:

1. Strong-model list: start with Qwen3-8B-Base only; Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B-base as a fast-follow once the pipeline works end-to-end. Confirm licensing for redistribution of sampled text (Gemma terms in particular).
2. Cluster labeling: agent-assisted labels are hypotheses, not ground truth — surfaced in the report as such, and the coverage verdict must come from #4934 BPB gap, not from cluster size.
3. Do not commit sampled text to the repo; write to `gs://marin-us-central2/experiments/coverage_sampling/` and register via `ExecutorStep`.
4. Preflight: 10–50k samples per model, truncated at 2k tokens. Cost estimate ~1 TPU-hour per model on v5p-8 for generation, plus CPU-only clustering.

Open question for maintainer before I start: should the strong-model sampler reuse `rl.rollout_worker` (heavier, battery-included) or a new thin client on `inference_ctx.vllm` (lighter, no RL coupling)? Leaning toward the latter to avoid pulling RL deps into the eval path.

- I added a latent-topic expansion-mode switch so we can expand from the original discovery prompt instead of the converged short stub.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: `r2` completed, and the expansion-mode ablation did not materially improve the bigram path.

Result:
- Job: `/dlwh/coverage-gap-vocab-bigram-smoke-r2`
- Experiment page: https://marin.community/data-browser/experiment?path=gs%3A//marin-us-central1/experiments/exp_coverage_gap_discovery-5de081.json

- Completed successfully on April 24, 2026 at 3:40 PM PDT.

Comparison vs `r1`:
- `r1` (`discovered_topic` expansion): `48/64` unique completions overall.
- `r2` (`discovery_prompt` expansion): `45/64` unique completions overall.
- The selected topic shortlist is effectively the same between the two runs; representative topics are still things like:
  - `state of matter is determined by the balance between the kinetic energy`
  - `The term expenses identifier typically refers to a unique`
  - `A nickname marketplace is a platform where individuals can buy`
- `r2` keeps the original bigram prompt as the expansion seed (for example `Physical aggregate`, `expenses identifier`, `nickname marketplace`), but the resulting completions still snap to the same generic explanatory continuations.

Current read:
- Tokenizer-derived bigrams are a real topic-agnostic prompt family, but they are not yet producing the unknown-unknown behavior we want.
- The failure mode is now stable across both expansion modes: Qwen maps many plausible two-word seeds into high-prior explanatory/documentary templates rather than revealing recurring latent domains across prompts.

Next likely move:
- Stop selecting by per-prompt support and instead rank by recurrence across different prompt families.
- Or add a much weaker lexical launch family (e.g. unigram / punctuation / structural fragments) plus a cross-prompt novelty filter, because the current bigrams appear too semantically committed.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Additional read on the vocab-bigram runs: the opening-token collapse is real in the raw discovery samples, not just an artifact of topic extraction.

From `r2` (`gs://marin-us-central1/evaluation/coverage_sampling/Qwen--Qwen3-8B-Base-coverage-gap-discovery-latent_topic-6c786d45-971b43/`):
- 43 / 48 discovery prompts had the same first whitespace token in at least 75% of their 16 discovery samples.
- 41 / 48 had the same first two whitespace tokens in at least 75% of samples.
- 32 / 48 were still collapsed through the first three tokens at that threshold.

Concrete examples:
- `Physical aggregate` -> all 16 discovery samples start with `state of matter ...`
- `expenses identifier` -> all 16 start with `The term "expenses identifier" ...`
- `Parliament attacks` -> all 16 start with `the government for its handling ...`

This makes the current read sharper:
- the bigram path is not failing because of summary truncation alone;
- Qwen is assigning extremely peaked next-token distributions to these bare noun-phrase prompts;
- that means we probably need a weaker launch family or a scorer that ignores the generic explanatory preamble and compares later divergence instead.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Decision: the tokenizer-vocab bigram line is a dead end for #5006's actual goal.

Why:
- `r1` and `r2` both completed successfully, so this is not an infra or TPU-plumbing problem.
- Switching expansion mode did not help: `r1` had `48/64` unique completions overall, `r2` had `45/64`.
- The discovered topic shortlist was effectively unchanged between the two runs.
- The raw discovery samples themselves are heavily collapsed at the beginning:
  - `43/48` bigram prompts had the same first token in at least `75%` of discovery samples
  - `41/48` had the same first two tokens at that threshold
  - `32/48` were still collapsed through the first three tokens
- Representative failures are stable across both runs:
  - `Physical aggregate` -> `state of matter ...`
  - `expenses identifier` -> `The term "expenses identifier" ...`
  - `Parliament attacks` -> `the government for its handling ...`

Current read:
- Content-word bigrams are already too semantically committed for the unknown-unknown objective.
- Qwen maps them into very peaked explanatory/article continuations, so they do not reveal cross-prompt latent domains in the way we want.
- This should be recorded as a negative result and not tuned indefinitely.

If the search continues, the next branch should be something weaker than content-word bigrams or a scorer that explicitly discounts the generic explanatory preamble. But the tokenizer-vocab bigram path itself is not worth more time.

spillover_issues.title: [evals] Use strong-model sampling to discover coverage gaps

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
Design doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LVfMDHRBKBk_Bn9PY1J9Lb_MYwdUTFP5PkX2br25TNg/edit?tab=t.izhzsywzorld (owner is updating it; this issue is the summary and coordination record).

**TL;DR.** Given one expert model E built from the Snowball student B, compare how much of E's gain each transfer method recovers and at what cost: SFT on E's traces, SFT on rejection-sampled E traces, and on-policy distillation (OPD) from E. Benchmark: CruxEval, training on the test prompts. Status: E is training; no arm has run yet.

**Models.** Student B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`. E = B after full SFT on GLM 5.3 traces (recipe from marin#9775: fresh AdamH state, frozen router biases). E keeps B's tokenizer and chat template. Every arm starts from B.

**Benchmark.** CruxEval (800 Python functions; input prediction and output prediction scored separately by executing the assertion). MATH500 was dropped because B already scores 89.8% there. Both CruxEval tasks are trained and reported separately.

**Teacher gate (done).** Under the frozen evaluator, B scores 55.4% input / 57.8% output. GLM 5.3 on the identical 1,600 prompts scores 94.0% / 90.5% (1,600/1,600 answered, none truncated). GLM also scores 84.4% on MMLU-Pro and 79.3% on GPQA-Diamond against B's prior 43.7 / 43.1, kept as fallback benchmarks.

**Frozen evaluator.** Marin `experiments.evaluation.cli launch` with Evalchemy `c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2`, vLLM on H100x8 (DP8 + EP8), `max_model_len` 32768, `max_gen_toks` 30720, `enable_thinking: true`, reasoning parser `grug`. Configs and pitfalls: https://gist.github.com/ksagar1030/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71. One correction found on the way: Evalchemy's chat client sends no temperature, top_p or seed, and B's `generation_config.json` sets none, so every run samples at vLLM's default (temperature 1.0, unseeded). Single-pass noise on 800 problems is about ±3.5 points; final candidates get two passes.

**Building E (in progress).** 1,454 GLM CruxEval traces that pass execution and carry reasoning (751 input, 703 output), rendered in B's native format: reasoning, then `<|end_think|>`, then the answer. 592k supervised tokens per epoch, longest row 22,835 tokens. First run: LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 273 updates, 32 H100s; exports after updates 92, 183 and 273. Other learning rates only if this run fails the gate. W&B: `marin-community/cruxeval-transfer-133`. Gate: E ≥ B + 10 points on both CruxEval tasks with no GSM8K drop beyond noise (B: 90.4).

**Arms (planned, all from B, matched prompt budget, same LR/epoch sweep for the SFT arms as for OPD).**
- Generate once from E: temperature 1.0, 8 samples per prompt, both directions, execution-graded.
- SFT-unfiltered: first 4 samples per prompt, correct or not.
- SFT-RS: up to 4 correct samples per prompt (rejection sampling, after arXiv 2610.04272, which closed Open-MOPD's 5.5-point OPD–SFT gap to 0.5 this way). Prompts with no correct sample drop out and are counted.
- OPD: on-policy distillation from E with the MarinSkyRL MOPD stack.

**Reporting.** For each arm: CruxEval input and output accuracy, the fraction of the E − B gap recovered, GPU-hours, prompts consumed, and GSM8K as the collapse check. Caveat that applies to every arm: training on the test prompts can transfer memorized answers as well as skill; SFT-RS is the most exposed.

**Not in scope.** Weight merging (needs RL-trained experts that share B's init; none exist) and transfer from the older Snowball experts (none beats B under the matched eval).

**Decision log.**
- 2026-10-06: matched eval of B and the existing experts (E6, E17a, E18, SWE, Stage-3) on MATH500/GSM8K; none beats B, so no promotion to teacher.
- 2026-10-07: MATH500 near ceiling for B → CruxEval chosen; MMLU-Pro and GPQA-D measured as fallbacks.
- 2026-10-07: full SFT over LoRA for building E; LoRA kept as the fallback if full SFT collapses out-of-domain.
- 2026-10-07: rejection-sampled SFT added as a third arm.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Teacher training and three transfer arms make this a gated experiment. As of 23:29 UTC, the owner has submitted the W&B-corrected teacher retry; startup, optimizer progress, and export remain unconfirmed ([latest status](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6048938002)). No open PR targets #9920, while the owner is already preparing the recipe on `task/133`; the earlier coding-teacher spike [#9528](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9528) ended without a usable MOPD transfer result.

**Relevant code**
- [`experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494) — shared SFT specification and training setup
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150) — versioned SkyRL experiment and export contract
- [`experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147) — shared evaluation launch path

# Proposed Fix

1. Follow the submitted teacher retry through a completed update, full training, and verified HF exports. Evaluate the planned exports with the frozen CruxEval/GSM8K configuration. Stop the transfer arms unless E clears the stated +10-point gate on both CruxEval directions without a GSM8K drop beyond noise.
2. Pin E, B, prompt IDs, tokenizer/template, grader, evaluator, and one eight-sample-per-prompt teacher generation artifact. Build unfiltered SFT from samples 1–4 and rejection-sampled SFT from up to four execution-correct samples. Record missing-correct-sample prompts, actual supervised tokens, and teacher-generation GPU-hours; a matched prompt set alone does not equalize training tokens.
3. Start OPD from the same B and prompts. Check teacher/student token-score alignment and one update plus export before the full run. Match the planned sweep and student update budget across arms, and record teacher-scoring GPU-hours separately.
4. Evaluate every selected arm twice with the same pinned evaluator on CruxEval input, CruxEval output, and GSM8K. Report each arm's accuracy, `(arm − B) / (E − B)` per direction, run-to-run spread, prompts and tokens consumed, and total GPU-hours. Label gains as transfer on the trained test prompts; this protocol cannot establish held-out generalization.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Export failure, confirmed on main. `train_lm.py` sets the converter's `reference_checkpoint` to `initialize_from_hf`, which for this run is a regional S3 copy of B. The HF export hook calls `save_pretrained` without `save_reference_code`, so it resolves to True for Snowball (its config class is not a `transformers` one). `_save_code_local` then calls raw `hf_hub_download` on the S3 URI and fails. The copy runs before the config, tokenizer and shard index are written, so the step-91 directory is not a usable checkpoint. `train_lm` exposes no switch for this.

Routes: (1) plumb `save_reference_code` through `AdaptorExportConfig` → `save_hf_checkpoint_callback` → `save_pretrained` and set it False (B's repo has no code files, so nothing is lost); (2) make `_save_code_local` URL-aware like the load paths (`_patch_hf_hub_download`, plus `snapshot_download`), the proper shared fix, as a follow-up. Retry decision pending with marten.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Correction to the response-shape note above, stating only what is observed.

Source: each run's `results_CruxEval.json` → `task_outcomes.CruxEval.completion_response_summary` and `failure_counts`, written by Evalchemy `c131e5ab` (`eval/completion_response.py`, `eval/robust_api.py`). A response is classified from the served reply's `content`, `reasoning_content` (as split by the `grug` reasoning parser) and `finish_reason`: `reasoning_and_final` (both non-empty), `final` (content only), `reasoning_only` (reasoning only, not length-capped), `reasoning_only_truncated` (reasoning only and `finish_reason == "length"`), `empty`. `malformed_model_response` = responses with no final content. Scorers receive reasoning and content combined, so a response with no final content is graded on its reasoning text.

Observed: B has 1,110/1,600 responses with no final content (1,085 reasoning-only, 25 of them length-capped); E step 272 has 94 (90 + 4). Raw responses are not retained in the record, so the mechanism (unclosed think block, parser split, or both) is not established, and the short-think/visible-CoT shape of the GLM traces is a plausible but unisolated cause of the change. The paired gains are end-to-end scored performance under this evaluator, not an isolated measure of code reasoning.

`reasoning_only_truncated` counts length caps only within the reasoning-only class; a length-capped response that still has final content is counted as `final` or `reasoning_and_final`. It is therefore a lower bound on length caps, not a total.

The last-checkpoint drops in RS-SFT (input) and OPD (output) are each supported by two passes but one training run; see the selection paragraph for the statistical limits.

Deviations from the plan in the issue body.

- Plain SFT used one sample per prompt (E's sample 0, 1,600 rows), and RS-SFT used the first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows), instead of up to 4 samples per prompt. Uncovered prompts stayed in the eval denominator.
- No LR or epoch sweep was run for any arm; every arm used LR 1e-6 and 4 epochs, with per-epoch checkpoints as the only sweep.
- OPD used 4 rollouts per prompt, so its prompt epochs are not token- or compute-matched to the SFT arms.
- GSM8K and MATH500 are both reported as collapse checks (the plan named GSM8K only).

Material failures and fixes.

- Levanter could not HF-export from an S3 reference checkpoint; fixed by plumbing `hf_save_reference_code=False`.
- MarinSkyRL accepted teachers only as HF repo ids; added staging of the teacher from S3. The export-only job's config inherited the run's distillation objective, which requires a teacher the export job does not start, so the export failed at config validation; the fix drops the distillation block from the export config. Learner nodes ran out of host memory at checkpoint save with 512 GB; the full run reserved 1024 GB.
- MarinSkyRL does not convert checkpoints to HF format during training; it writes a small export request per checkpoint, and the conversion is a separate 4-node export-only job (about 14–15 H100-h each).
- The Marin eval runner keeps the serve address it first resolved. When the serve job is preempted and re-registers on another host, the eval loops on connection errors until its timeout. Two RS eval groups were lost this way and relaunched as fresh groups; no partial outputs were reused. Not fixed yet.
- Evalchemy sends no temperature or seed, so every run samples at vLLM's default. One GSM8K run failed Evalchemy's preflight request 9 s after the serve registered (server disconnected); relaunched alone, it passed.
- GPQA-D (41.9%, needs an HF token and a 28,672-token generation cap) and MMLU-Pro (44.1%) were measured on B while choosing the benchmark, as fallbacks in case CruxEval failed the teacher gate; they were not used further.

spillover_issues.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |
| d2048 | 11 | 11,264 | 20,072 | 926B | 1.2B |
| **d6144 (hero)** | 11 | 11,264 | 390,139 | **18.0T** | 22.8B |

comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

🤖 Scaling-ladder analysis for the **535B-A23B, 18T-token** hero. The ladder trains one uniform hero EP recipe at five widths; four rungs finished and the d2048 rung crashed at ~81%. Fitting a power law across the rungs (`L = 1.5 + A·C^-α`, compute excludes lm_head) and extrapolating to the hero's compute predicts a final **dropless paloma macro-loss ≈ 2.04**.

**Hero prediction by training percentile** — the four measured rungs plus the d6144 hero prediction at every 5% (dashed/hollow = extrapolated).
![hero prediction by percentile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/hero_prediction_by_percentile.png)

**Per-5% scaling-law fits (log-log)** — one power-law fit per training fraction; the crimson points trace the hero prediction out to hero-scale compute, ending at 2.039 @100%.
![scaling law fits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_scaling_laws.png)

**Method check** — a linear extrapolation from each finished rung's 60–80% window predicts its own 100% dropless macro-loss to within ~0.003–0.004 (consistently a hair optimistic, since the curve flattens under cosine decay).
![60-80 extrapolation vs actual](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_extrapolation_60_80.png)

**Full-granularity training cross-entropy** — every step, with the datamix phase-2 boundary at 80% (a small loss bump is visible in every rung at that point).
![training cross-entropy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_train_ce_fullres.png)

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. I agree this probably needs larger-scale ablations to judge properly.

comments.author: yonromai
comments.body:
🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

spillover_issues.author: bethehand
spillover_issues.body: Hi @ClassicLarry @dlwh, To add uncertainty to the Aug 19 pre-registration in #8435, I made an independent forecast of the hero's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` (4K eval packing). It is frozen at 58% of training and uses only public data. **Result:** median **2.035**, 80% interval [2.023, 2.047], 95% [2.016, 2.054]. The Aug 19 pre-registration (2.039) sits at our 68th percentile, so the run looks on track for it. A finish near 2.10 looks very unlikely. **Method in brief** - The ladder is used only for the remaining drop from now to the end. The level comes from the hero's own post-swap evals, which makes the forecast nearly independent of the floor E. - Backtests set the drift persistence, the method error and an allowance for distance-dependent bias. They use held-out ladder rungs and the 67B-A2B run (#6044). In nested leave-one-out, the 80% intervals cover 14–15 of 16 held-out cases. - PTB gets its own term because of its noise and the exposures in #9874. A PTB-free companion target is forecast too: 2.047 [2.036, 2.059]. **One finding:** most of the 2.04 vs 2.10 gap comes from counting lm_head FLOPs in compute. On the H100 d768–d1536 runs, excluding them moves the fitted floor from 1.913 to 1.573 and the forecast from 2.116 to 2.037 (see the comment below for the refit's exact setting). **Pre-registration, code and scoring rules:** https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/prereg-v2-2026-10-09/preregistration_v2.md - The scoring rules were fixed in advance, including what happens if the context or the schedule changes. - This is v2. I revised v1 (median 2.045) the same day after re-auditing its backtests, on the same data. Both versions are tagged, and every change is listed. - I'll post a check-in at 70% and the scored comparison after the run ends.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body: A precision on the lm_head finding above: those numbers use the H100 d768–d1536 rungs, because the no-lm_head compute table I started from has no d512 entry. With the Oct 3 refit's exact setting (d512–d1536, one floor shared across both mixes and all 15 progress points), removing only the lm_head FLOPs moves the fitted floor from 1.858 to 1.630 (floors within 10% of the minimum SSE span 1.58–1.68) and the forecast from 2.100 to 2.056. So the compute convention accounts for about 0.044 of the 0.061 gap to the Aug 19 pre-registration, about 72%. d512 is where the convention matters most: counting lm_head multiplies its compute by 2.84, against 2.07 at d768 and 1.33 at d1536. Script and output: [addendum](https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/2c30e0d892531ae14c1b169e279ca3a8601a0286/addenda/2026-10-09_lm_head_exact_refit.md). The frozen forecast is unchanged.
